speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the last time this matter was up for debate I went into the issue of whether it was really necessary for the Government of Canada to be borrowing $29.5 billion, an amount equal to what was not too long ago our entire budget. Included in that total are amounts for contingencies which, for Members of the Opposition, represent a flashing red light. When the Government of Canada asks for over $4 billion more than its budgeted requirements, according to the Supplementary Estimates (B) and (A), there is reason to be concerned about whether the contingency amounts requested are totally necessary.
We on this side, on behalf of our constituents, expressed concern at the lack of priorities of this present Government. To compound this concern, we have obvious divisions within the Liberal Government and Cabinet on what should be the policy concerning financial accountability to the Canadian people and Parliament. On one hand we have a Budget brought down by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) which claims one thing. On the other hand we have members of Cabinet, who are now aspiring to become leader of their Party, expounding entirely different positions. That brings into question the credibility of this Government and Cabinet policies because there are obviously divisions within the Cabinet on just what direction this Government should take.
I would like to give a few examples of the contradictions between members of Cabinet and the policy as expounded in the Minister of Finance's Budget. One of the most crucial matters is that of economic development, and therefore we look to the Minister of State for Economic and Regional Development (Mr. Johnston). We find he is espousing certain things today which are not necessarily the position of the Government of the day as it proceeds with its request for $29.5
billion. I will give the House an example. On March 9 the Minister of State for Economic and Regional Development said:
I'm the last one to say that once you create a program it should stay there forever.
All programs can be improved. This question of universality-that's a buzzword which I don't even like to hear these days. The point is that social programs have to be married to the economic requirements of the country so that people use those programs to help themselves get back into the mainstream of economic activity.
He went on to say:
I think all Canadians understand that governments have to live within their means and that the only way of getting at the deficit is either more taxation or, on the other hand, cutting programs, or inflation, because that's another way governments traditionally have gotten rid of deficits in historic times.
If it is the intention of the Minister of State for Economic and Regional Development to cut the deficit, as quoted on March 9, why is the Government asking for $29.5 billion which would increase the deficit? Why is the Government requesting $4 billion more than it has fiscally spelled out in its 1984-85 requirements?
We can refer to other members of Cabinet to show that the Cabinet is obviously all over the place on what fiscal responsibility is. I maintain that no government can act any differently from any individual managing their household or any business person managing their business. When you spend more than you have on a continuing basis, sooner or later you are going to have to face reality. Money is going to cost more. When money costs more, inflation goes up and the value of the Canadian dollar goes down. As all caucus members in all political parties are aware, interest rates are now rising quite rapidly. Last week one-year Treasury bills moved from 10.44 per cent to 10.95 per cent interest, an increase of over 50 base points or one-half of 1 per cent.
The present net federal debt matures within about two and one-half years. It is essential following interest rate debt. The effect of last week's increase in interest rates alone increases the cost of carrying the $150 billion net debt of the country by $750 million. This little increase totally shatters all of the Budget figures of the Minister of Finance. This point should be well made by all members of the Opposition. The forecasts in the present Budget of the present Finance Minister are already out of date and we are still debating a borrowing law for $29.5 billion which is $4 billion more than the Government really needs.
To explain the differences of opinion within the Cabinet, I would like to quote a statement of the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Munro) made on

November 7, 1982. At a Liberal Party biennial policy convention, "bleeding heart Munro" supported a motion that we eliminate universality. He said:
The Government is wasting millions of dollars by sending monthly pension cheques to wealthy senior citizens and baby bonuses to families who do not need the money. Such funds should be redirected to help the most needy.
It is very damaging to the position espoused by the Liberal Party, that universality is here to stay, when statements like that are made within the Cabinet of the Liberal Government today by the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. They require some clarification from the Government as to what the policy is. Now that the Minister of State for Economic and Regional Development and the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development are travelling throughout the country telling people that what the Government is doing today is not right, it behooves us in the Opposition to confirm their positions and ask the Government of Canada what it will do about it.
Back in the early 1970s the Minister of State for Economic and Regional Development produced a book which is dedicated, to use the words of the Minister:
-to all Canadians who share my belief that Canada, with its beauty, its [DOT]resources, its people, and its legal-political heritage, could be a country of unequalled opportunity and happiness, were it not for too much taxation, too strong a bureaucracy, too much government, too much welfare, too many politicians, and too few statesmen.
There are so many inconsistencies in statements by Ministers today that one wonders if a Finance Minister who brings down a Budget calling for a projected debt of the country of over $31 billion and a borrowing requirement of some $29.5 billion is really fiscally accountable to the Canadian people.
Another article for The Toronto Start last year written by the same Minister of State for Economic and Regional Development states:
What we really require in Canada is solid fiscal reform on the revenue and expenditure sides to make our system more efficient and equitable. The taxing mechanism itself must be readjusted. At the same time we must address ourselves to the expenditure side, attacking inefficiencies and specific superfluous programs on a department-by-department basis. Wielding the big axe on programs across the board may have some political appeal but it's impractical and inefficient.
If I go into a few of the matters that need to be addressed by this Parliament, I think I would be repeating the Minister. We should occasionally look at some of our Crown corporations which were alluded to by the Minister of State for Economic and Regional Development as needing some cut-backs. We should look at Canada Post. The advertising costs in the post office are rising faster than the postal rates. Advertising costs are projected at $2 million in fiscal year 1983. According to Canada Post Corporation President Michael Warren, this will at least double to $4 million or $5 million in fiscal year 1984. The post office spent $500,000 to explain postal rate increases implemented in the spring of 1983.
Let us look at transport for a moment. Mirabel Airport has appropriately adopted a white elephant as its symbol. This unnecessary and unwanted airport has cost the taxpayers of
Canada a total of $841 million to date, including construction costs of $514 million and total operating costs of $327 million. In the last fiscal year 1982-83, Mirabel lost $35 million compared to a $43 million profit as Lester B. Pearson International Airport. I think we should rename Mirabel Airport "Pierre Elliott Trudeau Airport".
Out of 336 ministerial JetStar flights in the first seven months of 1982, 44 per cent were to transport Cabinet Ministers to and from their ridings. The estimated cost of this, based on Transport Canada charges of $ 1,000 per hour, is $300,000. Air Canada sent 20 executives to California for a $600 a day medical examination.
Let me deal with Petro-Canada and take a moment to point out a couple of matters that have recently developed with that Crown corporation. Petro-Canada is considered to be the "Big Brother" watching over consumers in Canada and trying to protect them. It has now entered into signed reciprocal trading arrangements with the Seven Sisters. This is a case of Big Brother joining the Seven Sisters in an effort to protect Canadian consumers. What are these reciprocal refinery agreements, some of them long term, 15 years or more, doing to Canadian consumers today when they go to buy gas at the pumps? They are forcing up the price of gas at the whim and fancy of our protector, Petro-Canada. I think it is time for the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Chretien)-

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1984-85 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to participate in the debate on Bill C-21, the borrowing authority Bill. This is not a routine piece of legislation but with the number of times we have debated the question of government borrowing over the years we tend to think it becomes routine. It is, though, one of the most important pieces of legislation before this House. The debate today is a debate on whether or not we are giving the Government authority to borrow moneys sufficient to finance the deficit, a deficit of 31.5 billion this year. It is a debate also on the implications of Government borrowing money of that magnitude.
I want to start by asking a very simple question of Hon. Members. Is there anybody in this House who wants to go through another recession like the one we went through in 1981-82, where employment in Canada dropped by over 5 per cent, where industrial production dropped by about 17.5 per cent, and where as a result thousands of businesses and many, many farms were lost? The answer is obviously no.
March 13, 1984

What we remember most about that period is the fact that interest rates were far higher than they should have been. Interest rates sky-rocketed during that period to between 22 per cent and 25 per cent. The reason was largely because of what went on in the United States and the very high interest rate policy followed there. Canada was going to have a deep recession regardless, but the effect of these high interest rates meant that the recession was far, far worse than it was in the United States. The unemployment rate in the United States went from 7 per cent to 10.5 per cent, whereas in Canada the unemployment rate went from 7 per cent to 13 per cent, almost double that of the U.S.
Why did this happen? What were the differences in Canada compared to the United States? We had the National Energy Program which totally undermined one of the most important industries in Canada. What about the way the Foreign Investment Review Agency was administered? There was the attitude toward investment, both domestic and foreign, and we had the 1981 Budget which raised taxes just at the point in time when the economy was falling into recession and we should have been reducing taxes. This caused a tremendous disruption in the economy. These were significant factors where deliberate economic policy in Canada added to the natural economic forces that were leading to a recession at that time. Our budgetary deficit was too high to give the Government the flexibility to offset the impact of higher interest rates in the United States or to follow a different economic course here in Canada. As a result, we were helpless as we watched the United States rates climb higher and higher. Canadian rates followed and in some cases were pushed even higher than those in the United States.
Today we are facing a similar scenario, Mr. Speaker. The Government still has not learned the lesson we suffered so dearly in 1981-82. It is likely that we will be facing a recession either later this year or early next year brought on by policies followed by the United States which we have no opportunity or flexibility to offset. All the ingredients are there. We have a slower recovery in Canada. Employment growth is far slower in Canada than in the United States. The unemployment rate in Canada has risen from 11.1 per cent to 11.3 per cent over the past two months. In the United States it has gone down from 8.0 per cent to 7.8 per cent. Business investment in Canada is flat. The latest figures for the Gross Domestic Product show that it has turned down.
By contrast, the United States economy is quite healthy. The unemployment rate, as I said, has gone down. Business investment, investment which creates tremendous numbers of jobs, in now projected to increase in 1984 by 12.8 per cent. That is the highest increase in real terms since 1966. The United States response is a classic one. It wants to temper this very healthy economy by leaning against it somewhat. The obvious response is to allow interest rates to move up ever so slightly to temper the boom and not let it get out of control.
Borrowing Authority Act
What is the Canadian response to our slow recovery? What would we expect? Are we allowing interest rates to fall somewhat because of the slow economy? Will we try to encourage business investment or the purchase of automobiles or houses by lowering interest rates? No. Interest rates are going up. They have risen about one percentage point over the past few weeks. Why are we moving in lockstep with the United States economy? This Canadian response is irrational and inappropriate. It will surely lead to the recession which we do not need at this time.
The Government says that we have no option, that United States rates are going up and that we have to follow because of our very close relationship to the U.S. economy. Surely that forces us to ask ourselves one question: How can we unhook ourselves from the United States economy? How can we gain a greater degree of independence of action? How can we distance ourselves somewhat from United States interest rates today when it is inappropriate for us to follow the same interest rate policy as the United States? Or, simply put, how can we avoid falling into the same trap that we did in 1981-82?
It is obvious that we cannot be totally independent from the United States. With 70 per cent of our trade and the great amount of integration between the two economies, we cannot become totally independent. However, we can achieve some independence and flexibility in our policy response when our economy is moving in a different direction. Right now we do not have that independence or flexibility. We have been described by some people as the tail on the end of the dog. I would describe it as being the flea on the end of the tail of the dog.
How can we achieve that flexibility and independence? I want to draw the attention of Hon. Members to the experience of the United Kingdom. In 1981 it took a policy decision to reduce its public sector borrowing requirement relative to total government spending by a significant amount. The result is that today its borrowing requirement or its deficit is about 8.5 billion pounds. That is roughly 6 per cent of over-all spending compared with about 30 per cent in Canada. Also it is about 2.6 per cent of its national income compared with about 8 per cent in Canada. The United Kingdom has moved differently from the United States because its economy is a little weaker. Previously its interest rates were very much the same as those in the United States, but we have seen a very interesting phenomenon over there: its interest rates have become unhooked from the United States ones.
I should like to give some figures on this. U.K. Government rates are 10.71 per cent. The U.S. Treasury rates are 12.05 per cent. United Kingdom corporate rates are 11.6 per cent and in the United States the corporate rates are 12.75 per cent. The bottom line of all this, when we take the different inflation rates into account, is that real interest rates in the United Kingdom are 4.9 per cent as against 7.2 per cent in the United States, a difference which is appropriate for the different performance of the two economies.

March 13, 1984
Borrowing Authority Act
The U.K.'s lower deficit has done two things for them. It has taken the pressure off interest rates. It has also given to the Chancellor of the Exchequer flexibility in his forthcoming budget to drop taxes or increase spending, depending on what he feels is appropriate at this time. He has that flexibility. He has that independence of action which we do not have at this time. The policy that they began in 1981 to reduce their deficit in a significant way has given them that flexibility to follow different policy approaches when that is appropriate.
There are other examples. I have just talked about the U.K. There is also the contrast between Germany and France, two countries living side by side with a fair amount of trade between them. It demonstrates that this is possible because of the better economic performance of the Germans relative to the French. They have been able to keep some distance between the two policy responses in those two countries.
That is the lesson of the Budget deficit that we have in Canada. The 31.5 billion deficit, plus the borrowing of the Crown corporations, is far higher proportionately than most other countries. Of the industrialized countries, only Italy is higher than us. Relative to the United States, we are about 50 per cent higher. That is why we must take action now on our deficit. We have to start taking those first steps today. With Bill C-21, this borrowing authority Bill, we are presented with that opportunity.
Let me summarize the economic costs of a higher deficit. First is the interest burden that all Canadians pay. The cost of the interest is $1,900 per taxpayer per year. Second, we have lost our flexibility within the Budget. One dollar out of three revenue dollars is spent on interest alone. One dollar out of five expenditure dollars is for interest alone. That is far too much. It reduces the dollars available for other programs. The third cost is that heavy government borrowing of the order of magnitude that the federal Government is borrowing today crowds out other productive investment, whether it is business investment or borrowings by individual Canadians to buy a car or a home. All of these are going to be squeezed back, particularly when you consider that over-all government borrowing today of $29.5 billion is about 92 per cent of the personal savings of individuals amounting to $32 billion.
The next point is that it forces foreign borrowing by the Government and by the Crown corporations directly through U.S. dollars, Swiss francs, German marks or whatever, or indirectly because of the amount of bonds that are purchased by individuals or institutions in other countries. Also, it forces provinces and corporations to move into foreign markets to borrow money when they cannot find that money in Canada. Canada today over-all is one of the largest international borrowers in the world, up in the big leagues with Mexico, Brazil and Argentina.
The next point is the high interest rate that are caused because of the concern of investors that these deficits are going to lead to higher interest rates and higher inflation. There has been a debate among economists that this is not so, but the fact is that in the real world investors have said that it is so
and have acted accordingly. That is one of the reasons real interest rates are as high as they are in Canada and the United States, the two countries with the most significant deficit problems.
The final point is the loss of confidence by investors in Canada and abroad. That is very clearly demonstrated in the weakness of the dollar, not just in these past few weeks. It is coming to a head right now, but this has been going on since 1976 when the dollar was $1.03. It is now 78 cents. That is purely and simply a lack of confidence in the financial management and performance of this economy. Today we are seeing the inevitable result of excessive government borrowing and government mismanagement. It is all tied together in that one figure, the level of the Canadian dollar in the foreign markets today.
These costs translate directly into lost jobs. It is a clear reason why today employment in Canada is still 139,000 jobs lower than it was at its peak in the middle of 1981, or 1.3 per cent. In the United States the comparable figure is 2,796,000 jobs, or 2.8 per cent higher than it was in the pre-recession peak. Where the disparity becomes even more serious is in full-time jobs. In the United States they are 1.7 per cent above the pre-recession peak. We are 3.7 per cent below that prerecession peak in terms of full-time jobs.
That contrast should be all that is necessary to tell the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) and Members of Parliament that the policies that this Government have been following are wrong, wrong, wrong. The place to change this policy direction must start with action on the deficit. The time to do it is now. It will give us more flexibility; not immediately, but it will start that process where we will be able to do the same as the U.K. has demonstrated in its performance in recent years.
Let us take advantage of the strong economic recovery in the United States. Let us move with them. If we can cut our deficit and be carried along by the momentum of the deficit in the United States, the pain here of reducing the deficit will be considerably less. Action today would give confidence to both Canadian and foreign investors to put money into this country, to give some upward lift to the Canadian dollar. That in itself would give the Bank of Canada some opportunity to relieve the pressure of interest rates and pressure on the Canadian dollar.
I stress that this will not happen overnight. It will take time. We have to start those steps today with a substantial reduction in the amount of borrowing requirements requested in this Bill. The reason why it will take time is that there is no confidence on the part of investors or individuals in the policy statements which this Government has made. Over the years we have heard various Ministers of Finance say: "We are going to hold government spending to the rate of growth of the national economy". Let us look at what has happened here. I want to give some examples. There have been four years in the past 14, one of which was a year of Conservative Government, when that actually took place.
Let us look at some of the times when it did not take place. In 1974 GNP went up by 19.4 per cent and government
March 13, 1984

spending went up by 29 per cent. The next year there was an 18.7 per cent increase in the GNP and government spending went up far higher than that. In 1977-78 it was 13 per cent as against 19.6; in 1981, 20.4 per cent as against 14.3 per cent; and in 1982, 18 per cent as against 5.2 per cent. No one believes what the Government is saying. That is why we have to show the public by our actions, not by words which have a very hollow ring to them.
Let me summarize the message that I have been putting forward to Members here today. We have to start today to take action. This was demonstrated clearly in the Estimates that we saw the other day. Spending controlled by legislation, so-called statutory spending, is up by 8.1 per cent. Discretionary spending, spending that can be controlled from year to year, is up 13.2 per cent. Therefore, there is no demonstration yet of the discipline needed to get this deficit under control.
The message to Canadians is that we have to reduce government borrowing. If we do reduce government borrowing, we will free up savings of Canadians for use for productive purposes, such as business investment, the purchase of cars, houses and the creation of jobs. We will reduce interest rates. There will be less pressure from the Government of Canada on the markets which will allow interest rates to come down. Most important, we will be able to increase the independence of action and flexibility of the Government of Canada in following policies which are appropriate to the Canadian economy, rather than being forced into slavishly following the United States when their economy is performing differently than ours. That is why we have to cut borrowing. That is why we as Members of Parliament have to take a hard line and tell this Government that it must cut back its borrowing for the good of all Canadians, for the health of our economy and the health of our society.

Mr. Speaker, I was very interested in listening to the Hon. Member, as I am whenever he speaks, but I would suggest to him that a great deal of a mumbo-jumbo type of analysis went on. Does the Hon. Member honestly believe that the whole problem with the economy can be wrapped around the deficit? He said that we should be reducing the deficit. I think all of us would agree that we want to see the deficit reduced. The specific question that he must answer is how it will be reduced. The Hon. Member said that we could reduce the deficit in many ways. Let us have him put some specifics on the table. Precisely how does he suggest that the deficit be reduced right now?
Second, does the Hon. Member realize that our economy is significantly different from that of the U.S. and the U.K.? Our economy is a resource-based economy. Has he looked at past history? Does he realize that a resource-based economy is typically hit harder in times of recession and that when facing world competition for those resources, it will have a difficult time restoring employment?
The main areas of unemployment in the country are in the resource industries. Those industries are facing stiff interna-

tional competition. What, perforce, would the Hon. Member suggest the Government do in order to make those resource-based industries more competitive with world competitors immediately? Those are a few of the questions I would like to put to the Hon. Member.

Mr. Speaker, perforce the Hon. Member would listen to my speech the next time and perforce he might learn something. Let me try to recall for him what I said in my speech. The Hon. Member said that all are in agreement with the need to reduce the deficit. Has he discussed with the Ministers the reasons it is important for us to reduce the deficit? I ask that question because I think it is important that we in the House do not get distracted by where we are going to cut. What is the most important point? It is of absolute importance to reduce the deficit so that we can have a healthier economy and deal with some of these other problems.
I am not suggesting to the House that the only problem we have is with the deficit, but I am saying, and I think the Hon. Member would agree with this, that it is the most important problem. Finding a solution to that problem will help us deal with some of the other problems with which we are faced.
The Hon. Member asked me where I would cut. If the Hon. Member had been in the House last week, he would know that I addressed that question then. If he would like he can check back in Hansard to see what I said.
Let me address the Hon. Member's second question which dealt with the fact that our economy is significantly different from that in the United States because our economy is a resource-based economy. That is precisely the point that I am making. The fact that our economy is different should be taken as the primary reason why we should be in a position to have the flexibility and independence to do the things we need to do for our economy without having to follow what happens in the United States. If we have a deficit of $30 billion and we have spending of $100 billion, 30 per cent of that is deficit spending. When we are spending one dollar out of three revenue dollars on interest and interest alone, what flexibility do we have to deal with the problems in the resource industries?
The Hon. Member asked me what I would do about these problems. Let me tell him what I would not do about them. I do not know how the Hon. Member can say to the House that our industry is resource based and we must be concerned about the loss of competitive positions for the two main industries. What happened to the mining industry 10 years ago? We took a series of steps which increased taxation in the mining industry just at the point in time when the competitive position of the mining industry relative to the rest of the world was beginning to suffer. That is when the Government significantly increased the tax load on that basic industry of the country.
What about the National Energy Program which began in 1981? The Hon. Member knows and I know that the steps taken by the Government led to a weakening in the energy industry of huge proportions which resulted in a loss of economic activity in that industry from which we are still

Bill C-21, Mr. Speaker, represents the largest borrowing authority ever to come before Parliament. The last largest Bill was, I believe, for $19 billion. This Bill asks for $29.5 billion. It is the eighth time this Parliament has been presented with a massive borrowing Bill. I believe the total borrowing works out to something like $103 billion.
My colleague, the Hon. Member who just spoke, talked about the tremendous burden this magnitude of borrowing imposes upon the Canadian economy and upon individual taxpayers. He indicated that the interest alone costs every taxpayer some $1,900 per year. Interesting as well is that the interest on the debt in the 1984-85 fiscal year will equal 4.7 per cent of Canada's Gross National Product, and this compares to a figure of 2 per cent when the current Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) first took office. That is a more than a doubling, Sir, and I believe that gives you some idea of what we are really faced with.
Another way of putting this, Mr. Speaker, is that in the fiscal year 1968-69, it required one out of every nine tax dollars to service the debt. Today, as a consequence of the successive deficits and the current irresponsibility of this Government, it takes one out of every three tax dollars to service
March 13, 1984

the deficit. Two disturbing thoughts emerge from this, Mr. Speaker. First of all, I am sure the public, particularly those people who are thoughtful and are concerned about the economic future of this country, have the impression that spending is clearly out of control and that the Government is not treating their tax dollars with any degree of respect. It has gotten so bad that the Government cannot even predict accurately. The budgetary deficit for this fiscal year, according to the former Minister of Finance, was supposed to be something in the order of $11 billion. It is instead $31.5 billion. So there was a mistake in calculation of $20 billion. That really goes not augur well for generating any confidence in the minds of the average Canadian.
This Government is so impaired, so drunk with spending, that it should lose its licence for life. I feel in the minds of people there is a sense of unfairness, a feeling that somehow the Government is not only spending unwisely, but it is being very unfair in the way in which taxpayers' dollars are being distributed throughout the country. There is a sense that there is discrimination and inequity in the distribution of the people's money. We know of the tremendous amount of money which is used for political purposes, the porkbarrelling, so to speak.
What emerges in the minds of the Canadian public is that there are really two classes of unemployed people in this country. There is regional discrimination, and the result of that, Sir, is regional disharmony and division. In some cases it creates a genuine feeling of disgust. One only has to look at articles which have been written, some recent and some not so recent. I will quote from an article by Brian Fox of Southam News in the July 30 edition of The Citizen. It outlines in detail the Special Recovery Projects. The headline reads "Liberal ridings win at handout time". The article begins:
The federal government has been using its pump-priming $2.4 billion capital works program to pour millions of dollars into Liberal ridings and the backyards of influential cabinet ministers.
It continues:
Politics undoubtedly has been a major factor in determining where these valuable federal funds would be spent.
For example, in Nova Scotia $25.4 million has been budgeted to improve 31 small harbors. Of those, 19 are in Cape Breton Highlands-Canso, held by Allan MacEachen, now minister of external affairs and deputy prime minister.
Interestingly, MacEachen is one of nine Liberal ministers on the sub-committee which approves the siting of the projects.
Of the remaining 12 harbors, 10 are in other Liberal ridings and the remaining two are in Progressive Conservative territory.
To date, those two harbor improvements are the only projects that directly benefit PC ridings.
The article concludes:
In true Liberal fashion, these goodies are timed for the middle of the byelection campaign-
That sums of the kind of feeling of unfairness and inequity which pervades the country. This is the feeling of people who are strapped and finding life very difficult when they see this kind of money thrown around simply for political gain. And it will probably continue. It will probably get worse. An article in
Borrowing Authority Act
Edmonton's The Journal talks about the secret film which unveils Liberal strategy, and I quote from the article:
The 30-minute Film implies throughout that the Liberals will use taxpayers' money to woo key electoral groups-women, youth, the urban middle income groups and ethnic voters.
In addition to Canadians being discriminated against, I believe they feel a sense of "being had", being conned by this Government with their own money through advertising, through straight porkbarrelling and through the kind of seductive practices which will be contained in this 30-minute film. The total picture is that respect for the institution of Parliament, respect for government and respect for the departments of government is being eroded very dramatically. If we couple that with what is going on in the Department of National Revenue and the high-handed, Gestapo-type tactics which are being employed by that Department to extract every last bit of blood out of the taxpayer, there is a real feeling of disgust and anger out there.
In summary, Mr. Speaker, it means that there is something dramatically wrong and something must change. If we are going to have a voluntary income tax system, there is going to have to be some improvement in the integrity of that system. There must be some improvement in terms of accountability so that this institution, Parliament, will have some control over the expenditure of taxpayers' dollars.
The Government fails to recognize that what it is spending here is not money that falls from the sky, it is the people's money. The lack of respect, indeed the disrespect, this Government has had over the years for the people's money is really at the root of the problem.
On successive borrowing authority Bills our Party has tried to zero in on the need to reduce waste. We have identified many areas where in our opinion there is waste and extravagance. We have tried to identify areas where excessive government expenditure could be reduced. We have tried to identify programs which we believe have outlived their usefulness and should be reassessed. We have supported the Auditor General in his desire to ensure money is spent on the basis of adequate value received-comprehensive analysis. What we find disturbing, Mr. Speaker, is that when these areas are identified this Government uses distortion, fear and hysteria. When you question any expenditure the Government immediately says: "Oh, the Tories are going to cut this and that". That is very irresponsible, Mr. Speaker. How can you, in a rational way, attack this problem which has built up over the years? Why can we not have a rational debate on this issue?
We have recommended that a sort of no holds barred committee be formed to get right into the nitty-gritty of the Government's expenditure program. But the Government pooh-poohs the idea. That is only one suggestion for getting to the bottom of some of these things, and I am sure there are others. But we know the Government will not go that route because it would restrict its ability to porkbarrel, to cajole the voter into supporting the Government. It would restrict the

March 13, 1984
Borrowing Authority Act
Government's ability to con people with their own money, to buy votes.
The Special Employment Initiatives Program is a clear example of discrimination in the most crass manner that one could ever envision. We have waste and unproductive investments, and all of it adds up to a massive burden on the producers of this country.
We are hearing a lot about the new Liberalism, the new era of Liberalism of the 1980s. If the slick media campaign being unveiled is any indication where the new Liberalism is going to take us, then we can only expect that we are going to have the same kind of thing. The former Minister of Multiculturalism, in his expressions about ballyhoo and manipulative tactics, gave an accurate description of this Government today. I sense it will be an accurate description of the Government under a new leader, irrespective of who that leader might be.
I would like to give you a couple of examples, Mr. Speaker, to illustrate clearly the motivation of the Government in its abuse of the taxpayers' dollar. First of all, there was an announcement by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Axworthy) some time ago concerning the expenditure of some $306 million for the establishment of four new maintenance centres for VIA Rail. There was one in each of Winnipeg, Halifax, Montreal and Toronto. I want to talk about the Montreal facility because I think that is a real can of worms in this project.
At present VIA Rail rents a facility under a three-year lease with a one-year renewal option over a six-year period. It is paying roughly $3 a square foot, with 600,000 square feet of available space although it is using only 70,000 square feet. The facility is pretty good. It was built by Hawker Siddeley. However, rather than maintaining that facility or purchasing it, which it could do for something in the order of $11 million, and renovating it for probably $14 million to $15 million, for a total cost of $25 million, what do we see here? The Minister of Transport announces a commitment to build a facility worth $147 million. Add in the equipment and interior improvements and we are really talking about a figure in the order of close to $200 million. But they have a facility there now which the Government could have for roughly $25 million. That is the kind of abuse and irresponsibility we are talking about.
My colleague from Peterborough talked about Mirabel, and I could talk about the aborted airport at Pickering. We know that when the Mirabel airport revolving fund was renegotiated the airport was losing something in the order of $52 million per year. With the write-down and rearrangement of the airport revolving fund the losses were cut, simply through a book transaction, to some $20 million or $25 million. On August 24, 1982 the Windsor Star said: "The elephant is still white but now there is hope. After seven years of failure new federal plans may be able to revive Mirabel". It is not being revived, Mr. Speaker.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1984-85 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext: What's $500 million?

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1984-85 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
What is $500 million? What's a billion? That is really the attitude. It does not matter because it is not the Government's money, it is the people's money. This Government, any government, is charged with the responsibility of preserving and ensuring those dollars are spent wisely and in a productive fashion. The taxpayer should not be abused.
When you look at this piling up of deficit upon deficit, Mr. Speaker, we could liken it to a family living beyond its means. Year after year after year they take out a new mortgage on their home to buy groceries and pay for their vacation and gasoline for the car. I am very interested in the remarks of the Minister of State for Economic and Regional Development (Mr. Johnston), who is running for the leadership. On March 9 he said that he thought all Canadians understand that Governments have to live within their means and the only way of getting at the deficit is either through more taxation or, on the other hand, cutting programs. Or through inflation, because that is another way governments traditionally have gotten rid of deficits in historic times.
Well, Mr. Speaker, we have a situation where the Government is really mortgaging the homes of Canadians, Canadians today and Canadians in the future. This has had a major impact on the nation's confidence, and a major impact on our ability to engage in productive investment which would increase the size of our Gross National Product. This is at the root of the problem of medicare and social programs which are under attack. It goes back to the issue of poor economic management. Mismanagement is really the buzz word for the Government's performance.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1984-85 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member will appreciate that the amount of borrowing required depends to a large extent on the growth projections in taxation and so on in the country. In his Budget the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) forecast a growth of 4.9 per cent or 5 per cents, depending on how you read it. In the House yesterday the Minister said that the average projection for growth by economic agencies was 4.6 per cent. I know the Member studies economics and economic forecasts. Has he ever seen any growth projections by a private forecaster issued in January, February or March of this year that indicated any growth projection of 4.6 per cent, let alone an average of 4.6 per cent? Is the fact of the matter that the only growth projections overproduced this year have been in the order of 3.3 per cent, similar to the projection produced by the Conference Board?

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1984-85 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I and my colleagues on this side of the House would prefer to follow the projections of
March 13, 1984

the Conference Board of Canada because it has consistently been more accurate than the Government. The Minister of Finance should have some credibility. We should be able to believe him. The Government does have the resources and facilities with which to make accurate projections. However, the Minister said that in 1983-84 we would have a budgetary deficit of $11.8 billion. It turned out to be 31.5 billion. I submit that does not provide much credibility to any figures which flow from the mouth of the Minister of Finance.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1984-85 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I know that the Hon. Member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski) comes from a constituency which has many farmers and ranchers. That group of people are heavily dependent on capital, and often borrowed capital. If the Government gets another $29 billion of borrowing authority, does the Member have any concerns or fears that that might have an impact on inflation and interest rates? Of what detriment might that be to the people in his constituency?

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1984-85 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it will be a very major detriment. In The Globe and Mail this morning it was reported that agriculture is in depression. The number of bankruptcies is 58 per cent higher this year than last year. Last year there were 488 farm bankruptcies registered. That is about 400 per cent more than in 1979. That four-year period is significant because that is when the Government was returned to power. Naturally the increased borrowing will cause pressure upon the capital markets and will drive up interest rates. It will have an impact upon inflation as well.
Our Party advanced a 10-point agricultural program a year ago. We have renewed those principles time and again. One of them is the provision of at least $100 million to allow farmers who are locked into these high interest rates to bail themselves out. We also support the establishment of farm finance review boards which would assist farmers as an arbitrator functioning through the auspices of the Farm Credit Corporation offices, in negotiating with banks. We have also advanced other initiatives such as the reduction of the 9 per cent sales tax on farm fuels and fuels used by fishermen. In other words, we believe it is counter-productive for the federal Government to impose a heavy tax burden on the producers of food.
I could elaborate further. The fact is that there was nothing in the last Budget to assist and motivate optimism and hope in the agricultural community. The Government is looking after retired farmers but is certainly not looking after the young farmers and the farmers who find themselves in severe difficulty at the present time.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1984-85 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask a question of the Hon. Member for Vegreville. When the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) took office in 1968 about $12 billion was required to look after the affairs of the nation. At that time we numbered something like 20 million people. This year we have seen a Budget tabled which calls for more than $98 billion, and with the supplementaries it may well run to about $103 billion, to look after a nation which now numbers about 25 million people. Does the Hon. Member feel these excesses were
Borrowing Authority Act
necessary? Why does he believe it takes more than eight times the amount to look after five million extra Canadians?

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member is correct. When I came to the House in 1968 the Budget was $11 billion or $12 billion. Today it is $100 billion. Is that money needed? I guess there is room for some increases. I believe it really illustrates the growing intervention of government into the lives and economic activities of Canadians.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1984-85 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1984-85 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext: We see potential leaders running across the country espousing a new Conservatism and a new Liberalism. That is really what they are talking about. speakeroldname: Mr. Jean-Guy Dubois (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1984-85 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the shouts from the Official Opposition are most meaningful! I hear my colleague from Mission-Port Moody (Mr. St. Germain) who is also in the House and speaks very well, both in French and English. He just nodded to me, and I must say I am very pleased to see him in the House this morning. Well, Mr. Speaker, about the situation concerning Bill C-21, an Act to provide borrowing authority, we are hearing a lot of comments from the Opposition to the effect that the Government's deficit is a disgrace, that it must be brought down and that spending must be rationalized. However, we do not hear many comments telling us what programs should be cut. Of course, one of the Opposition Members has said that perhaps it would be a good thing to reduce or cut universality of health care, and it was the former Minister of Finance of the Progressive Conservative Government, that short-lived Conservative Government of 1979, who had dared to say so, and his comments were printed in the press. He was reprimanded by his Leader who said these services must not be touched. So it is all very well to make comments and get excited here in the House and say that the Budget deficit is a very serious thing and that we must do something about the fact that Canadians, according to the Opposition, are in difficulty. Mr. Speaker, there are many Government programs that are administered either by the federal Government or jointly by both levels of government. Obviously, there are many programs that require funding, and consequently, the Canadian Government, on the basis of its economic or social policies, must respond to the needs of Canadians. Whether we are talking about the spouse's allowance, the guaranteed income supplement or a pension system, the Government must act in response to the needs of Canadians. That is why in his Budget Speech, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) approached this subject that is very important to Canadians who are eligible for these benefits. He said in his
2038

March 13, 1984
Borrowing Authority Act
speech, on page 14 of the Budget papers, that about 750,000 single senior citizens, three-quarters of whom are women, will benefit from the increase in the guaranteed income supplement. The Minister goes on to say that the additional Government support will amount to $460 million in a full year. The important thing is that Canadians approve of these social measures. And as far as the health care system is concerned, the polls show that Canadians generally favour the present system, and consequently the Canadian Government must continue in that direction.
About the deficit-because we have to finance these programs if Canadians are to benefit-we must ask ourselves: Where does the deficit come from? It seems that a large part of the increase in the deficit is due to increased public debt charges. Only a relatively small portion of the expected increase in the deficit will be due to official measures taken by the Government. However, the Government is prepared to accept an increase in the deficit in order to provide strong support for the economy. When the April 1983 Budget was brought down, at some point, perhaps a few weeks before, economists were asking the Government to increase the deficit if it had to, provided it released funds for job creation and for stimulating economic activity. They said that stimulating the economy would automatically reduce the deficit. Therefore, after reading the usual articles on the economy in general, we can say that our deficit is a cyclical, not a structural deficit. This means that if the number of jobs continues to increase, Opposition Members will say there was an increase in the unemployment rate over the last month. We must not forget that although 54,000 new jobs were created, there were also 75,000 Canadians entering the labour market for the first time.
What we have to do is adopt incentive measures that will automatically reduce the deficit and create jobs. Once jobs are created, economic activity will reduce the number of people drawing unemployment insurance benefits and thus reduce public spending. Similarly, the amount of corporate tax and sales tax collected will increase as well. Furthermore, once the planned increase in the tax rate, partly required to finance the incentive measures announced in the April Budget, becomes effective, that too will help bring down the deficit.
In this connection, Mr. Speaker, I would like to discuss our job creation programs. When we talk about job creation, we are talking about the employment situation of young people, men and women and in fact the population in general, but when we look at the statistics, we try to focus on the situation of our young people. For instance, right now we are preparing for the Summer Canada Program. For the fiscal year 1984-85, the Canadian Government wants to give Summer Canada a budget of $70 million, so that 27,000 Canadians will be able to take part in this program and we will be able to help these people during the summer. There is also the Canada Works
Program and Section 38, which will help people go back to work. The Career Acess Program is also very important and also requires considerable funding. If we look at the budgets for 1983-84 for job creation, and I am referring to Canada Works, a grand total of $812.8 million has been earmarked for it. Benefit costs will amount to $66.5 million and the actual program will have a budget of $614.3 million. There will also be an unemployment insurance budget of $123 million. As far as participation in terms of person-years is concerned, there will be a total of 250,000 jobs which equals 58.4 person-years of work. The important thing is that we have all these job creation programs, including Canada Works, LEAD, Career Access. If we take the case of Career Access, this program will help people who have been unemployed for some time and who, in some cases, may have exhausted their unemployment insurance benefits and are looking for a job. For 1983-84, the Career Access Program will have a grand total of $115,000 million.
Mr. Speaker, all these programs have to be financed. If we want to reduce our deficit, we must provide a stimulus for workers and employers to create jobs. In the Budget Speech of February 1984 and its predecessor of April 1983, the Minister said that the private sector, with the incentives provided by the Canadian Government, is a creator of jobs. We have a number of temporary programs. For instance, in 1982-83, we introduced the NEED Program. There were other programs that existed at the time, including the CCDP, Canada Community Development Projects. We injected money into the system to put Canadians to work and reduce the amount of unemployment insurance benefits being paid. We wanted to keep these people in the labour force and keep the economy going.
If we look at the NEED Program-and I am thinking more specifically of my own riding-last year, Mr. Speaker, under this program which was announced when we returned to the House around October 20, if I remember correctly, when the Minister of Finance brought down his Budget on October 27, 1982, the sum of $170 million had been earmarked for the Province of Quebec. At that time, there was an agreement with the Government of Quebec, which was concluded in December 1982. The agreement was broken, however, and now both levels of Government are pursuing their own objectives, and in the riding of Lotbiniere we were able to get $1.5 million-in other words, people presented projects and job creation was the result.
The important thing was that these programs such as NEED and Canada Works were made available to the private sector in order to stimulate employment. When an employer in the private sector hires a person who is in a job creation program, he may, if he is satisfied, decide to employ that person on a permanent basis, thus possibly taking someone off the welfare rolls or off unemployment insurance. As I said earlier, economic activity stimulated by the Government has an impact on employment. When, with the incentives made
March 13, 1984

available to them by the Government, employers are employing people who had left the labour market, these programmes, for instance in the riding of Lotbiniere, are beneficial.
Through the Canada Community Development Projects for 1982-83, the riding of Lotbiniere received over one million dollars. That year, as I said earlier, we were able to get $1.5 million under the NEED Program. For Summer Canada, we got nearly $200,000. The Canada Works budget for the riding of Lotbiniere is one million dollars, and this year, Summer Canada will have a budget of $147,000.
Mr. Speaker, these are job creation programs, programs that provide incentives for employment. If we consider the entirely temporary aspect of summer job creation programs, the effect will, of course, be felt only over a short period, because students are concerned here.
But, Mr. Speaker, we do have to work if we are going to finance all those programs. It is important to set those funds aside as an incentive to encourage employers to hire those people. The Career Access Program, to which I referred earlier, is a commendable undertaking, and the Canada Manpower Centres in every riding are open to employers and people who want to submit their applications. All those job creation programs are designed to help the private sector hire young people and others who have been seeking employment unsuccessfully for weeks. Other programs are specifically open to women or the handicapped. I heard somebody on the other side say that we have been experiencing problems and running a huge deficit over the past 15 years as a result of the Government's massive intervention in the private sector. When it comes to providing incentives, this Government is just as concerned as the private sector. I do not think we have any lesson to learn from Members opposite, particularly not from the Official Opposition. There is no doubt that we have to cooperate with them, as we have been doing for many years, Mr. Speaker, and we have been working even closer together since the Budgets of April and February were brought down. Never before have we had as much consultation as has been the case since the current Minister of Finance came on the scene. There was some, but not that much with the private sector. What were the priorities of the private sector in terms of job creation and lower deficits? As I was saying at the outset of my remarks, some economists pointed out in April 1983 that perhaps the Government should not be overly concerned about the deficit, that it should offer incentives, stress the importance of job creation and realize that it was more urgent to turn the economy around without constantly worrying about the deficit and thus steer the country right out of the doldrums and the recession we were experiencing. That is exactly what happened. There are other economic sectors where program financing is needed, and that is why we have to seek borrowing authority regularly at the end of each fiscal year. Invariably, we hear the same arguments from Opposition Members who
Borrowing Authority Act
take us to task for financial mismanagement and urge us to slash expenditures here, there and everywhere.
Mr. Speaker, we simply cannot ignore the fact that these are hard times and that we must face up to the heavy financial commitments which those various programs entail. Should we tighten the purse strings of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, even though that Department does make financial contributions to job creation programs? Should we reduce the funds earmarked for social programs or for the Guaranteed Income Supplement? Should we set less money aside for health insurance or post-secondary education which is financed by the Government to the tune of about 60 per cent? All those benefits are built into the system, people ask for them and want them maintained. I suggest that we must act responsibly and fill those needs, while at the same time providing financial incentives to create jobs and respond to the plight of the unemployed. And then, Mr. Speaker, the Government took the initiative of its 6 and 5 program. We said to the public sector: Listen, we have to face reality, we are going through an economic recession and the Government must be among those that set an example in terms of salary increases, we simply cannot afford to go beyond certain limits. After that, of course, we urged the private sector to adopt a similar approach. In my opinion, that policy had an extraordinary impact throughout the country. Some of the unions were perhaps reluctant at first, but then they wondered whether it would not be better to warn their members that the economic situation was bleak, that interest rates were quite high, and that they might be well advised to protect their jobs while waiting for an economic upturn and better prospects for income stabilization.
I believe that this fact was very readily accepted by the business community and the unions and in proof of this we have seen companies negotiate with their employees wage increases which allowed them to meet their obligations. This has been a period of co-operation and of increased awareness about existing conditions, and I believe that labour has now come a long way and seen the need to show some self-control and to be realistic considering existing economic conditions. I believe that labour has understood this very well. And when the Government decided to set an example in this area with respect to the implementation of its 6 and 5 policy, it was able to use some of the money thus saved to provide certain benefits for the vital sectors of our economy such as the building industry by offering purchasers of new or existing housing subsidies of up to $3,000 which were used to help create employment. People often say that when the building industry is in good health, so is the rest of the economy. I think that it was important to have such programs, Mr. Speaker. However, the incentives and assistance programs which we now have must be funded. As I was saying earlier, if we maintain these incentives and continue to create jobs, then the deficit will go

March 13, 1984
Borrowing Authority Act
down. I therefore believe that the House should support this Bill and approve the borrowing authority requested by the Government.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1984-85 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext: Are there any questions or comments?

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1984-85 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have been listening to the Hon. Member's speech. I noted with some interest that he said one of the main reasons for the borrowing of money was the creation of work. He listed a number of programs, Canada Works, New Horizons, community development programs and so forth.
Bearing in mind that what we are doing now is talking about $29 billion, or a $102 billion deficit, does the Hon. Member not recognize that every time we borrow money of that kind we rob the borrowing market, which results in very stiff competition for the private sector? This causes pressure to increase both inflation and interest rates. In turn a negative impact on capital construction occurs in the private sector throughout the country and in fact it robs the country of jobs. While on the one hand the Hon. Member is trying to claim that you borrow money to create jobs, basically borrowing money destroys permanent job creation in the factories in favour of whitewashing local cemeteries. In other words, a job is created once and then destroyed thereafter.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1984-85 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I cannot agree with what the Hon. Member has said about the situation. The economists were saying after the April 1983 budget and also after last February's budget that the Government had to provide some incentives in spite of the deficit. This is what has been done since April 1983, and, whatever the Hon. Member might say, the rate of inflation has gone down considerably from between 10 and 11 per cent to about 6 per cent. It has fluctuated from one month to the next. While the Government made use of the borrowing authority which was approved last year, the inflation rate has gone down, incentives have been provided to create jobs and labour demands for wage increases have been reasonable. This is because, whatever the Hon. Member may say, there has prevailed a climate of confidence and it has been possible to lay some emphasis on job creation in the private sector with the assistance of the Government and because of all this the inflation rate has gone down and the economic activity has increased. When they saw that the economy was on the road to recovery, instead of keeping their money in the bank, Canadians began to reinvest in the economy in order to accelerate this recovery. As a consequence thereof, while many economists say that the deficit should be reduced, existing programs, in the areas of job creation, financial assistance and social legislation, for instance, must continue to be funded. If we had no unemployment insurance plan no social security programs, where would we be now, Mr. Speaker? Indeed, we
have lived through the recent recession. Contrary to the Hon. Member's opinion, I believe that incentives, reasonable wage increases and job creation programs, have shown the general public that the Government wanted to co-operate with the private sector and that this did not stop the economy from recovering as everything proves it has been doing since last year.
I therefore believe that we must continue to honour our financial commitments and to do what we have been doing since October 1982, April 1983 and even June 1982 by way of the 6 and 5 program. This is why the budget brought down in February stated that the restrictions would be lifted but that wage increases would have to be reasonable. As concerns the confidence of Canadians and the fact that they were afraid that interest rates would increase, this is why, especially to help the building industry, the mortgage guarantee program was proposed. I believe that with programs and incentives such as those we shall be able to keep inflation at a reasonable level and continue to encourage people to invest in the Canadian economy and in their own businesses, because economic recovery is a worldwide phenomenon, and in this way, the Canadian people will continue to have their place in the sun.

Mr. Speaker, the best example of this is, having in mind the economy, if we refer to a small business or a farm .. . Let us take the example of a farm. The Hon. Member wants to speak about farms! I could go on for quite a
March 13, 1984

while on the subject. We know what the situation is in Alberta and we know what the situation was under the Crow rate. The Hon. Member was certainly against its being changed! Let us have an example, Mr. Speaker. To reply more specifically to the question, I can say that all our general services and programs, at the post-secondary level, for instance, will produce assets, and while our children will inherit some indebtedness, if the economic situation continues to improve as it is now doing, the public debt will decrease accordingly. I am sure that, with all the facilities we have, with all our export and import programs, with the markets which we are developing through our industrial, business and job creation programs, our children will be able to face the future. We shall put at their disposal the ways and means of coping with American and European competition and of producing on our own markets, so that while we may have some debts, we shall also have the assets and the wealth to meet these debts. I have therefore no worries as far as the future generations are concerned, Mr. Speaker.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1984-85 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate in the debate on Bill C-21, an Act to provide borrowing authority. In the Budget of February 15, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) proposed expenditures of some $98 billion. The Minister projected borrowing requirements of $25.5 billion and a few days later the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Gray) comes forward and asks for a borrowing authority of $29.5 billion, an additional $4 billion in less than three weeks. Like many Hon. Members on this side, I never cease to be amazed by the cynicism of the Liberal Government.
Why does the Minister ask for a borrowing authority for $29.5 billion rather than the $25.5 billion projected in the Budget? 1 think that begs some questions. Is the Budget some mere device rather than the primary economic document of the nation? Did the Minister suddenly discover that the Government needs an extra $4 billion? How will this $4 billion be used? Will it be used as petty cash for the Government? Is the Minister angling for a status like C. D. Howe had when he stated; "What's a mere billion"? The President of the Trea-
Borrowing Authority Act
sury Board wants $4 billion. Is he trying to attain a higher status?
As Members of Parliament we have the final responsibility for the administration of public funds. The amount is mind-boggling, almost $100 billion. My constituents understand the revenue side very well. They understand the tax structure and that Revenue Canada is very efficient in gathering tax moneys. A small business in my riding has found itself in difficulty because of a receivership. They are subcontractors who had amounts owing to them of somewhere in the neighbourhood of $80,000. They are unable to receive their moneys, but Revenue Canada is on top of them requesting their tax money. If they pursue this, this small cabinet business will have to close. That is the kind of tactic being used. This is what is happening to the small businessman.
What about the corporate structure, the large multinationals which are able to write off large amounts of tax? Canadians do not understand why the Government is asking for this $4 billion. Perhaps this money will be used to subsidize the transportation of western coal to eastern Canadian markets. Why not look at something like this? We have repeatedly asked this question in the House. Over 4,000 lakes in Ontario are dying because of the sulphuric acid in the air.
We import 16 million tons of dirty coal from the United States. This costs almost $ 1 billion a year. That dirty coal has a sulphur content 800 per cent higher than western Canadian coal. What is wrong with a program whereby the supplying province, the consuming province and the federal Government work together to create jobs in western Canadian coal fields, supplying central Canadian markets and stopping $1 billion from leaving this country each year as well as putting thousands of Canadians back to work?
Those are the kinds of programs we should be looking at. What does this Government do? It joins with the province in a project in northeast British Columbia which is costing billions of dollars. There is now a subsidy for the project. A study which has been conducted indicates that if that coal is shipped at less than $100 a ton, it will have to be subsidized. It is currently being sold at $84 a ton. Hundreds of miners are being laid off in southeastern British Columbia for short periods of time. We are vying for the same market, using taxpayers' dollars for a program that puts Canadians out of work in southeastern British Columbia. Does that make economic sense?
The Government asks for an additional $4 billion. It certainly will not get my consent for that kind of program. If the Government looks at something sensible that will create not only a clean environment but keep $1 billion a year from leaving the country and creates employment here, it will have my support.
My constituents are concerned about this $4 billion. Will it be used as another slush fund to elect Liberals? My constituents have difficulty with the gigantic tax expenditures mandated by this Government. Knock out a few of those tax expendi-

March 13, 1984
Borrowing Authority Act
tures and the Government would not need this extra $4 billion. Why not drop the measure in the Budget that allows lawyers and doctors to pay less than their fair share of taxes as a result of RRSPs? Why not cap the amount Canadians can lock away tax-free in RRSPs? Why not start taxing corporations and banks at a level equal to what ordinary Canadians pay?
In the booklet Budget in brief there is reference to energy and resource taxes. It states that the incremental oil revenue tax will be deferred for an additional year, to June 1, 1985. This alone will save the oil companies $190 million. Our small business people and farmers are being pushed to the limit, going into bankruptcy right across this country, at the same time as we are giving the rich oil companies even bigger breaks. Through the Petroleum Incentives Program the Government will come up with as much as 93 cents on the dollar for exploration programs. Where, oh where, is it going to end? There is no commitment that Canadian products will be used or that Canadians will be hired, thereby alleviating our unemployment situation.
I also want to comment on the mortgage insurance program. What a scam this Government is putting forward! This mortgage insurance program will ensure that the banks get their interest rates. That is exactly what it will do. When you walk into the bank, the manager will say to you: "You are running pretty tight here; I do not think we would consider making this loan unless you have an insurance policy to ensure you can carry it through". Is that the kind of program we want? When the mortgage is due in three years, the interest rate may have gone up another 6 per cent or 7 per cent. This person would have to start again at that rate.
This program will only benefit the banks. If the mortgagor wants to sell his home, he will not be able to sell his insurance program, so up will go the interest rate. Who will buy at those kinds of interest rates? The Government knows that interest rates are going up yet it brings in this scam to cover up, telling the people not to worry, that they will be able to take out an insurance policy. What a joke!
I want to comment on the employment programs of this Government. It has a role to play and it must start playing it seriously, particularly in the area of technological change. In Japan it was found that there is a need to develop an early warning system in the form of flow of information about the planned introduction of new technologies. They have a program which studies the workplace to the year 1990. They have communications with their employees about their plans and programs, what they are doing in the workplace. They know the number of people who will be retiring and the replacements that will be needed. They are starting to train the replacements. Until we come up with that kind of program, we will have serious economic development programs. If we do not recognize that very soon, other countries will take over the major trade and we will be in an even more serious situation than we are today. It is unfortunate this Government uses patchwork programs, throwing money in any direction to try to carry it through so that it can be re-elected.
I want to refer for a moment to the comments made by the Hon. Member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie). He stated in Vancouver that if the Conservatives were in government, they would take a serious look at pensions and family allowances and possibly at bringing back the means test. I hope they never get in government if they are looking at those kinds of policies. I hope this Government will recognize that the B.C. Conservatives have taken over the government of that province, whether they call themselves Social Crediters or Conservatives. They are cutting education programs. Busloads of secondary school children have to travel 35 kilometres to school. Classrooms are being closed and they are being bussed to other areas. That is a shame. It should not happen with the resources that we have and it can only be related to the mismanagement of the Government of Canada.

AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, government Members continually say that we are in a recovery period. That does not include what I am sure would be an equal number of farmers who voluntarily liquidated and sold out.
The Government continually refuses to recognize this problem. Canadian farmers are in trouble. The Government continually refuses requests for emergency funds, implementation of agri-bonds, more Farm Credit Corporation dollars, lower interest rates, and reduction of energy taxes. It is time government Members paid attention. What has to happen before they wake up? It is time for the Minister of

subtopic: MAGDALEN ISLANDS SEAL HUNT
MAGDALEN ISLANDS SEAL HUNT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to tell the House how deeply I regret last weekend's events on the Magdalen Islands, which are part of my riding.
I cannot help condemning the members of the animal welfare group for their provocative actions.
