subtopic: SELECTION OF LIBERAL PARTY LEADERSHIP CONVENTION SITE
SELECTION OF LIBERAL PARTY LEADERSHIP CONVENTION SITE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Liberal members are like bottlecaps on an assembly line. Singular in purpose, they scour for power. Hour by hour, they drink and bathe in power. Who can tell, Sir, what happens to Liberal Members when they go walking in a snow storm? What destiny do they witness in a frozen sky? How badly does a winter blizzard numb their neurons?
Edmonton's Liberal alderman, Julian Kiniski, lobbied to encourage that Edmonton might host the upcoming Liberal leadership convention. That indeed was a laudable objective, for which I commend him highly. However, when Edmonton was not awarded the convention, he playacted animated anger, claiming that he had never been so furious in his life, and alleging that the reason Edmonton did not receive the convention was because the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mulroney) did not assure that the Government would not be defeated during the convention.
That was some ferocious blizzard within which Liberal Members took a walk which caused them to reason that,
because of the over-population in China, the alfalfa production at the Prince Edward Island weather station will cause the Grand Canyon to fill with uranium and there will be nuclear war, and therefore high school will be let out early. That was some blizzard, Sir.
In the past when conventions have been held for the NDP or the Conservative Party, the Government, by tradition, has recessed the House. Are we to expect that it would forget to recess the House for its own convention? Does Kiniski and other Grits expect that Parliament would convene with no government Members present? Kiniski is naive. Such meetings do take place, but they are not called Parliament. That, Sir, is a caucus.

subtopic: PROVINCE'S REFUSAL TO ALLOCATE NON-PROFIT HOUSING UNITS TO TORONTO
PROVINCE'S REFUSAL TO ALLOCATE NON-PROFIT HOUSING UNITS TO TORONTO
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, CMHC's federal allocation for public non-profit housing was announced in January. Under this important program Ontario gets 1,400 new housing units. However, the Province of Ontario which administers this program refuses to allocate any of these units to either Toronto or Metro Toronto. Furthermore, the provincial Minister of Housing, Claude Bennett, is using flippant and very political language to try to assure the people of Toronto and hide his personal indifference.
The reality behind this situation is quite a different story. Single parents, seniors, pensioners, disabled people, and low-income earners across the City of Toronto are being denied access to new housing. The long waiting lists in that city are getting even longer. Now the Government of Ontario, which has traditionally neglected its housing responsibilities, is offering not only financial neglect but adding to that a very serious geographic neglect.
In the biggest city in the country, public social housing is grinding to a halt. This is unconscionable. The Province of Ontario's Minister of Housing must be condemned for this insensitivity and his flippant arrogance.

subtopic: CALL FOR NATIONAL JOB CREATION STRATEGY
CALL FOR NATIONAL JOB CREATION STRATEGY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in Canada 85 per cent of the people work, and 15 per cent of the people do not work. This is unfair and is quietly killing those who do not work.
In the Province of British Columbia 25 per cent of the young people are unemployed. We will face a lost generation, and that is a tragedy. Unemployment is the major problem in Canada today, and I call for a national commitment to full employment. I call for jobs for all by 1989.

March 13, 1984
Now, more than ever, Canada needs new ideas. I propose that we take the $13 billion from unemployment insurance payments, the $8 billion which is given to the oil companies, tax those fat cat banks, and use that money to create a national job-creation strategy. We should begin by upgrading, not downgrading, our educational system, so that we have the finest in the world, and we should create jobs for all by 1990.
In 1960, Mr. Speaker, I remember John F. Kennedy saying that America would put a man on the moon by the end of the decade. Let us make a commitment to put all Canadians, especially young Canadians, back to work and have full employment by the end of the 1980s.

subtopic: EXCHANGE VALUE OF DOLLAR
EXCHANGE VALUE OF DOLLAR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, economic confidence in a nation is reflected by the value of its currency. The plunging Canadian dollar illustrates the lack of confidence which the market holds in the decaying Liberal Government and the lack-lustre quality of the various candidates seeking leadership of that sinking ship.
Exchange problems have been compounded by the amazing behaviour of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde). One day he does not care to what low levels the dollar sinks; the next, he instructs the Bank of Canada to buy Canadian dollars in any amount in order to camouflage the market response to his misguided policies. Tomorrow, as he again pirouettes with considerably less elegance, might I say, than his erstwhile leader, we face the inevitability of higher interest rates. The Canadian dollar will not cease its drift, nor will it stabilize, until the Canadian people have ousted the present Government and replaced it with a Conservative Government in which all can have confidence.

subtopic: SUGGESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF MEDICAL INJURIES COMPENSATION BOARD

speakeroldname: Mr. Stanley Hudecki (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Defence):

subtopic: SUGGESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF MEDICAL INJURIES COMPENSATION BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at a recent conference of the Canadian Institute of Law and Medicine, Justice Richard Holland suggested setting up a medical injuries compensation board which would eliminate the need for medical malpractice lawsuits. Under this scheme patients would recover damages based upon the extent of their injuries, rather than having to prove medical negligence in court in order to win a monetary award. I, too, see merit in this recommendation, in view of the rapidly escalating costs of medical malpractice insurance premiums which have come about as a result of many judgments exceeding $ 1 million in personal injury suits.

A second reason is the presumption of guilt stigma which is attached to members of the medical profession charged with malpractice, even if they are innocent. Malpractice litigation is now truly a growth industry as lawyers are more prone to take court action in malpractice suits. The Canadian Medical Association must consider these recommendations and explore their implementation through the justice departments of provincial legislatures.

subtopic: REMOVAL OF STREET LETTER BOXES
REMOVAL OF STREET LETTER BOXES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for the past several weeks I have received many letters from concerned citizens in my riding of Timiskaming. The majority of these letters are from senior citizens who have written to me complaining about a relatively new Canada Post Corporation program involving the removal of street letter boxes.
In one particular area of Kirkland Lake a street box has been removed in the interests of post office efficiency and savings. However, what the post office does not seem to take into account when it removes these street boxes, are the hardships faced by senior citizens who used to rely on the corner box near their homes.
One lady wrote me and stated:
I am a woman, 76 years of age, and find it is hard, especially in the winter, to mail my letters, because I use a cane. I hate to ask anyone to go out of their way for me. I know there are a lot of elderly people in this district who write letters, so it must be a hardship for them to get their letters mailed.
Surely Canada Post, in its efforts to cut costs and increase efficiency, can retain a degree of compassion when implementing policies such as the street box removal plan. I urge the Minister responsible for Canada Post to ask the President of Canada Post to rethink his corporation's policy with respect to relocating street letter boxes. I urge Canada Post to consider the thousands of senior citizens in Timiskaming and throughout Canada who rely on the post office, and to reinstate street boxes in neighbourhoods where there is a high concentration of elderly people.

subtopic: TAXATION OF WORKERS' COMPENSATION BENEFITS
TAXATION OF WORKERS' COMPENSATION BENEFITS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on an important matter affecting those elderly Canadians who receive workers' compensation benefits following work place injuries. GIS benefits to the poorest elderly are being cut because the Government now treats these receipts as income rather than compensation.
This change was buried in an omnibus tax bill following the MacEachen and Lalonde Budgets, and slipped through almost
March 13, 1984

without notice. The change will mean more disabled workers are forced to subsist on incomes below the poverty line. The Government consistently refuses to increase old age pensions to eliminate poverty among the elderly, but must it begrudge the elderly the miserly sums they do receive? Why must benefits to the disabled be cut back?
This amendment is unwanted. Members on all sides have spoken against it. Even Revenue Canada, not noted for its generosity, has chosen to disregard the law and advises tax filers to ignore the change for most tax purposes.
We, in the New Democratic Party, call on the Government to table legislation immediately to ensure that GIS is not reduced by workers' compensation benefits. We are prepared to deal with such a bill as expeditiously as possible. One Minister has already advised the House that ministerial discussions on this matter are under way, but how long must the disabled suffer while the Ministers dither?

subtopic: FUNDING SOUGHT FOR P.E.I. ELECTRO-MECHANICAL TECHNOLOGY PROGRAM
FUNDING SOUGHT FOR P.E.I. ELECTRO-MECHANICAL TECHNOLOGY PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to discuss an issue brought to my attention by the President of the Architects' Association of P.E.I., concerning funding for an electro-mechanical technology program for Holland College, the community college of Prince Edward Island.
Holland College has made application to receive funding through the Skills Growth Fund offered by the Department of Employment and Immigration. The program the community college wishes to develop includes computer aided drafting, design, and manufacturing.
I share the sentiments expressed by the President of the Architects' Association in that there is a need for the development of technological skills. In an attempt to alleviate the employment problems faced by our youth, it is necessary to provide exposure at post-secondary institutions to equipment which will help accelerate the growth of design and manufacturing sectors.
New advancements in technology will bring within the grasp of small businesses new markets within Canada as well as abroad, and provide employment growth. With increased emphasis placed on new technology, a strong demand for education and retraining of the work force is created. If we wish to keep abreast of this growth, we must provide the necessary tools, equipment, and programs, to train our young people properly and provide an on-hands learning experience to which students all across the country are entitled.
I urge the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Roberts) to support this worth-while project for the Province of Prince Edward Island as it is an investment which will pay dividends not only for P.E.I. but for all Canada.

Mr. Speaker, the Liberals have lost all credibility. During the last 16 years the Grits have perpetrated policies upon the Canadian people resulting in one and a half million people being without work; a national debt which is 500 per cent higher than it was in 1968; thousands of farmers in a state of desperation, with 488 having gone bankrupt last year, and a program which will send most businesses in Banff into bankruptcy or receivership.
Now some of the Ministers are preaching solutions to the ruinous policies which they themselves imposed on the people. Well, let us look at the land rentals in Banff which are completely under the control of the Liberal Government. One business paid $300 in land rents in 1979. No business can raise its prices sufficiently to meet such gigantic increases, and the former Minister of the Environment who imposed the rents and the present Minister, refused to change them. Not carved in stone? Indeed! To re-elect the Grits would be like hiring the arsonist to put out the fire he started. Promises to change disastrous programs now, in a desperate attempt to stay in power, means nothing to the Canadian people who can no longer believe a word the Liberals say.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Economic and Regional Development. This would seem to me to be a totally inappropriate and wrong policy response at a time when unemployment is growing and when business investment, a part of our economy which is most affected adversely by high interest rates, is projected to have no growth at all in 1984. subtopic: COMPARISON WITH UNITED STATES ECONOMY
COMPARISON WITH UNITED STATES ECONOMY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, that is precisely the point I am making. Why is the Government allowing the interest rates to rise? Its unemployment rates are falling, ours is rising. Its business investment is rising to record levels; ours is flat. Its retail sales are up; ours are down.
It does not make any sense at all for us to have this situation in Canada where interest rates are allowed to rise. Is the Minister telling us there is no alternative, that the Government has no flexibility and no other options but simply to follow the policy of the United States lock-step, and watch our economy fall into the doldrums again?

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not think the Hon. Member is paying attention to the debate which is going on today, which is on the borrowing requirement. Is that not the reason why we have a weak dollar and the Government is being forced to let interest rates rise?

speechtext: I do not know what kind of an outburst that was, Mr. Speaker. We all know that one cannot borrow, and borrow, and borrow; that is precisely the point the Minister of Finance made. We have come through the most difficult recession this country has known since the 1930s.

subtopic: SIZE OF GOVERNMENT BORROWING
speechtext: Why was it difficult?

speakerposition: Minister of State for Economic and Regional Development; Minister of State for Science and Technology
subtopic: SIZE OF GOVERNMENT BORROWING
speechtext:
We know the effect on the deficit of the automatic stabilizers in our system. The Minister of Finance is taking steps to ensure effectively continued and sustained economic growth, which is the best way of getting the deficit under control through revenues which will accrue as a result. Therefore I am not quite sure what the Hon. Member's point is. If he is decrying the size of the deficit, welcome to the club. We have all been concerned about the deficit. We are also concerned about the recession, and the programs which have been absolutely necessary to sustain Canadians through this
March 13, 1984

period. That is in large measure why the deficit is where it is today.

subtopic: SIZE OF GOVERNMENT BORROWING
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I thought this putative leader had the answers. We certainly have not heard them today.

subtopic: LEVEL OF JOB CREATION

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (St. John's West):
subtopic: LEVEL OF JOB CREATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in an address called "New Financial Impediments to Economic Recovery", Mr. Mackness of the Bank of Nova Scotia points out that job creation, which was very rapid in the early stages of the Canadian recovery, has ground to a halt. Employment has increased at an annual rate of less than 1 per cent over the last six months compared to 5 per cent in the first eight months of recovery, and compared to U.S. job creation which is still surging ahead in excess of 5 per cent.
Why is it that in Canada our job creation is now less than 1 per cent in the last six months while in the U.S. it is 5 per cent? What policies does the Minister suggest which could bring us up at least to the level of the U.S.? What is he doing, rather than what is he saying?

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald J. Johnston (Minister of State for Economic and Regional Development and Minister of State for Science and Technology):
speakerposition: Minister of State for Economic and Regional Development; Minister of State for Science and Technology
subtopic: LEVEL OF JOB CREATION
speechtext: I wish I could do something for the Hon. Member who is wallowing in misery over there, Mr. Speaker.

subtopic: LEVEL OF JOB CREATION
speechtext: It is the 1.5 million unemployed who are wallowing in misery.

speakerposition: Minister of State for Economic and Regional Development; Minister of State for Science and Technology
subtopic: LEVEL OF JOB CREATION
speechtext: The fact is that this country has a record in job creation that is unexcelled.

subtopic: LEVEL OF JOB CREATION
speechtext: That is wrong.

speakerposition: Minister of State for Economic and Regional Development; Minister of State for Science and Technology
subtopic: LEVEL OF JOB CREATION
speechtext: We knew, and everyone forecast, that the very strong recovery, which far exceeded everyone's expectations, would begin to slow down. subtopic: MINES AND MINING
MINES AND MINING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Hon. Minister of Mines. Given the Government's concern over high unemployment and the weakness of the Canadian dollar due to capital outflow, and given the desire of all Canadians to reduce acid rain, can the Minister assure this House that, as a corrective measure
Oral Questions
addressing these problems, his Ministry has done its utmost to promote the use of high grade, low sulphur western Canadian coal which will create thousands of jobs, clean up the environment, and save $1 billion from leaving our country?

subtopic: MINES AND MINING
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, not only are we concerned about western Canada coal, but I can tell the Hon. Member that we have a study under way in the Department on the use of non-ferrous smelters, and we hope to be making some further announcements about that in the near future. subtopic: IMPORTATION OF UNITED STATES COAL
IMPORTATION OF UNITED STATES COAL
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, could the Minister then explain why, in 1983, central Canadian coal users continued importing 16 million tons of low-grade, high sulphur American coal, the use of which threatens some 48,000 lakes in Ontario? subtopic: IMPORTATION OF UNITED STATES COAL
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I can point to a number of initiatives where we have assisted western coal in British Columbia. For example, the largest part of our trade with Korea is in coal, and it is growing rapidly. We are making every attempt to export Canadian coal, and I think it is showing some results.

subtopic: NATIONAL REVENUE

speechtext: 1981 AUDIT OF FISHERMEN'S EARNINGS

speakeroldname: Hon. James A. McGrath (St. John's East):
subtopic: NATIONAL REVENUE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of National Revenue. According to the report commissioned by his predecessor, the Rowe report, during the audit of fishermen in Canada in 1981 the average earnings of Newfoundland fishermen were $7,481, and in Prince Edward Island $8,752. The poverty line in Canada as defined by StatsCan is $9,300 for a family of four, or $11,400 for a family of six.
Why did the Government, specifically his Department, conduct an audit of a group of people whose earnings were below the poverty line?

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre Bussieres (Minister of National Revenue):
subtopic: NATIONAL REVENUE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I suggest the Hon. Member is looking at this issue from the wrong angle. The way he directed his question would seem to imply that legislations such as the Income Tax Act

March 13, 1984
Oral Questions
which are Revenue Canada responsibilities should not apply to particular groups of individuals.
If the Hon. Member read the Rowe Report a little further, he would realize that Mr. Rowe indicated clearly that when penalties and fines are imposed following an audit, they are imposed in compliance with the legislation, and that when contributions are assessed, it is in conjunction with existing incomes. That is a truism. The figures which the Hon. Member has quoted, therefore, are average earnings and do not apply in all cases, which means that some individual earnings are higher, while some others are lower, and the tax rate for the former is greater than for the latter. His question, therefore, has nothing whatsoever to do with departmental responsibilities or the Income Tax legislation as it exists now.

subtopic: NATIONAL REVENUE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, judgement is the issue here. The Minister does not seem to be exercising that in his answer, and certainly not in his actions.

subtopic: ROWE REPORT FINDINGS

speakeroldname: Hon. James A. McGrath (St. John's East):
subtopic: ROWE REPORT FINDINGS
speechtext:
Is the Minister trying to justify to the House and the country an audit of a group of people whose income is clearly below the poverty line, some of whom have had third party attachments on them for as much as 60 per cent of their gross incomes? The rationale for the audit in the first instance was because of a mistake made by the Government, namely, a ground fish subsidy of 2.5 cents per pound which was paid for four years by the Government, on which not T-4 slips were issued.
Given all those circumstances, and the fact that the Government has had this report for over two years, why was a stop not put to that disgraceful audit?

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre Bussieres (Minister of National Revenue):
subtopic: ROWE REPORT FINDINGS

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member knows perfectly well that when the report was published, the audit had been terminated. The Hon. Member knows that. Furthermore, he knows perfectly well that a . . . Member should at least have the common decency to listen to the reply and show a little more intelligence in his understanding of the situation.
If assessments were made, this means that there was equivalent income. He is using an average figure as the basis for his claim that there should not be a tax audit. He knows perfectly well that this is a false premise.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT'S POWERS

subtopic: DEPARTMENT'S POWERS

subtopic: NON-APPEARANCE OF OFFICIALS BEFORE CONSERVATIVE PARTY TASK FORCE HEARINGS
NON-APPEARANCE OF OFFICIALS BEFORE CONSERVATIVE PARTY TASK FORCE HEARINGS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is for the Minister of National Revenue. In a letter dated February 24 to the Member for Wellington-Duff-erin-Simcoe the Minister gives reasons for the inability of his officials to testify. He says "the anonymity of public servants, and their political impartiality and loyalty" were at stake if they did testify. How does the Minister reconcile that reasoning with the fact that the Assistant Deputy Minister of Revenue for the western region appeared on Cross Country Checkup and gave a speech to the Chamber of Commerce where he made the most controversial of statements? Why can they appear on public radio and give speeches to Chambers of Commerce, and yet not speak to Members of Parliament?
[ Translation]

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre Bussieres (Minister of National Revenue):
subtopic: NON-APPEARANCE OF OFFICIALS BEFORE CONSERVATIVE PARTY TASK FORCE HEARINGS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member fails to see that he is daily undermining his own credibility by making statements that are based on pure fantasy.

March 13, 1984

subtopic: HOUSING
HOUSING
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister responsible for housing. In his absence I will direct it to the Minister of State for Finance, if I can get his attention. My question has to do with the spectre of high mortgage interest rates which is once again coming to haunt Canadian home owners. I would like to remind the Minister and the Government that those interest rates rose to an appalling 23 per cent just three years ago and thousands of Canadians lost their homes. What has the Government in mind now to prevent those interest rates from soaring out of sight, causing thousands more Canadians to lose their homes?

subtopic: HOUSING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not share the view of the Hon. Member that there is any likelihood of mortgage interest rates soaring out of sight in the time ahead. On the contrary, indications within the Canadian economy with regard to long term interest rates remain favourable. The recent modest increase in mortgage rates is not, in my view, indicative of any trend contrary to that favourable long term trend which I have indicated.
In any event the Hon. Member should bear in mind that in the recent Budget we have provided for a mortgage rate protection program which will assure a mortgage holder that he or she will not again experience the type of mortgage rates which we had in Canada a year or two ago.

subtopic: HOUSING
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Minister's response reminds me exactly of what his predecessor said when mortgage interest rates were around 12 per cent or 13 per cent in 1980.

subtopic: MORTGAGE INSURANCE SCHEME-AMOUNT OF PROTECTION FOR HOME OWNERS
MORTGAGE INSURANCE SCHEME-AMOUNT OF PROTECTION FOR HOME OWNERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to quote Mr. Peter Carter of Royal Bank mortgage and consumer services. He said: "People will only start to claim under the insurance program when interest rates-God forbid-reach the levels of 1981 again". The Minister does not need to be reminded that at that time mortgage interest rates were 23 per cent.
Will the Minister acknowledge that if the interest rates rise by 3 per cent the home owner who has this insurance will still end up paying 75 per cent of the increased mortgage costs out of his own pocket? Will he also undertake to persuade the Minister of Finance that the only real protection for home buyers and home owners is to have the Government require that banks set aside a specific portion of their lending portfolios for mortgages, at long term stable interest rates?

subtopic: MORTGAGE INSURANCE SCHEME-AMOUNT OF PROTECTION FOR HOME OWNERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Member opposite must know that the real protection against higher mortgage rates in Canada is the reduction in the level of inflation in Canada. In recent months in Canada
Oral Questions
we have seen a sharp decline in wage rate levels. We have seen wage settlements. We have seen a rapid increase in productivity. We have seen a moderation in cost increases in industry. These are the real factors which create protection against higher mortgage interest rates in Canada.
The Member opposite must also realize that in the Budget we not only provided a mortgage protection plan, but we offered a mortgage-backed securities scheme which should also ameliorate the circumstances in the mortgage market generally, and contribute to a limitation on the rates of mortgage in the time ahead.

subtopic: TOURISM
TOURISM
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister responsible for tourism. It is clear that the Liberal Government has neglected tourism over the past decade to the point that our tourist deficit has skyrocketed from a staggering $1.3 billion in 1982 to a record $2.1 billion in 1983. This has resulted in the incredible loss of 100,000 jobs last year alone. A lack of cost competitiveness in Canada is virtually pricing the tourism industry out of business, despite the low Canadian dollar vis-a-vis the American dollar. Can the Minister tell us what he is doing specifically to alleviate this very, very serious problem in our economy?

speakeroldname: Hon. David Smith (Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
subtopic: TOURISM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, specifically, we recently launched a television campaign directed toward Canadians, encouraging them to vacation in Canada. I am sure many Members will have seen this campaign, and I think it will have a beneficial result.
In addition, we will be launching a major television campaign in April all across the northern tier of the United States that is within a one day's drive to Canada. I am sure we will see a real turnaround in terms of the number of American visitors who will be coming to Canada.

subtopic: TOURISM
speechtext: I did not know the Minister was that naive. Surely he knows, as John Lawson of TIAC pointed out, that this increase in the advertising budget of $22 million does not get to the root of the problem but simply brings the advertising budget back to what it was a decade ago.

March 13, 1984

FISHERIES
subsubtopic: SEAL HUNT-REQUEST FOR BAN ON CLUBBING WHITE COAT PUPS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct my question to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans. As the Minister is aware, the fishing industry on the East and West Coasts, as well as in central Canada, is facing very serious marketing problems in the United Kingdom and the United States because of the seal issue. In view of the fact that the Newfoundland sealers decided last year not to hunt seal pups, and the sealers have again taken the same stand this year, backed up by the Newfoundland Government, will the federal Government, in the interest of protecting the over-all Canadian fishing industry, put a complete ban on the clubbing of white coat seal pups anywhere in Canada?

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre De Bane (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
subtopic: FISHERIES
subsubtopic: SEAL HUNT-REQUEST FOR BAN ON CLUBBING WHITE COAT PUPS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to remind the Hon. Member that the House of Commons has, in several instances, unanimously passed resolutions defending our sealers in Arctic Canada, Labrador, northern Quebec, and the Magdalen Islands. They were passed unanimously by the House. I assume that this is still the position of his Party.
Second, I would like to remind the Hon. Member that we are not dealing with rational people on this issue. We are dealing with fanatics who have been spreading lies about our fishermen and our sealers. I would ask the Hon. Member to reflect on what would be the reaction of those fanatical people if you give in on something which they have already destroyed themselves and if we should go to the point of declaring something illegal that, at this moment, is not happening in Canada because they have destroyed the market for our fishermen.

subtopic: FISHERIES
subsubtopic: SEAL HUNT-REQUEST FOR BAN ON CLUBBING WHITE COAT PUPS
speechtext: I would remind the Hon. Minister that this is the second year in which the Newfoundland fishermen have voluntarily withdrawn from the clubbing of white coats, and that we did support the position put forth a moment ago, as he stated. But times change. They will change after the next election. We are changing with the times.

subtopic: REQUEST THAT MINISTER LAUNCH PUBLICITY CAMPAIGN
REQUEST THAT MINISTER LAUNCH PUBLICITY CAMPAIGN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, will the Minister, in conjunction with the External Affairs Department, establish a publicity campaign to inform the world that Canadians no longer engage in the clubbing of white coats, or
seal pups, and will he inform the United Kingdom, and all the Europeans, at the same time that their fish quotas in Canadian waters will have to be reconsidered since each seal eats approximately a tonne and a half of fish per year?

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre De Bane (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
subtopic: REQUEST THAT MINISTER LAUNCH PUBLICITY CAMPAIGN
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I will certainly give serious consideration to all of the valuable suggestions of my hon. friend. On the other hand, I am happy to report to him that as of 2.45 p.m. today, the report that I have from my Department, which got in touch with every single important buyer of Canadian fish, is that not one of them will give into that blackmail because they realize that, if they give in on this issue, tomorrow there will be blackmail on the fur industry and other single issue causes, by people who are determined to blackmail. Last year they tried to destroy the market for the sealers and they did not succeed. This year they are trying to blackmail the fishermen. The buyers realize that if they give in to this group this year, next year it will be on another issue. It is in their own interest to resist any blackmail.

subtopic: NATIONAL REVENUE
NATIONAL REVENUE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of National Revenue. April 30 is fast approaching and workers getting tips are still facing the inequity of having to pay taxes on their total income while the Unemployment Insurance Commission is not collecting contributions accordingly. I know that the Minister had advised me to direct this question to the Minister of Finance, but in his absence, will the Minister of National Revenue tell us whether, in view of the date set for the filing of income tax returns, he has made any recommendations to correct this injustice, which he recognizes himself, and whether the Minister of Finance has responded favourably to suggestions for correcting it?

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre Bussieres (Minister of National Revenue):
subtopic: NATIONAL REVENUE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance has not provided me with any answer because I did not ask him the question. However, I must remind the Hon. Member that, as far as the Department of National Revenue is concerned, the declaration of tips is the responsibility of the workers themselves. This means that, before their tax returns have been filed, we do not know in advance the amount of tips they will declare.
The Hon. Member is certainly referring to the proposal made by the Quebec Government and he knows how strongly this proposal is still being challenged.
March 13, 1984

Oral Questions

subtopic: REQUEST FOR EXPLANATION
REQUEST FOR EXPLANATION
speechtext:
The Minister of National Revenue is aware that the Unemployment Insurance Commission regulations as applied by the Department of Employment are obviously being unfair considering the fact that the Department of Employment and Immigration is assessing the contributions of the worker who receives tips on the basis of his wages without his tips being taken into account.
The Minister is also aware that he is responsible for collecting the contributions and that many Canadians pay income tax without ever being entitled to the corresponding social benefit provided under the Unemployment Insurance Plan. The Minister is aware of all this and I would like him to explain why, since he is aware of this injustice, he has not already recommended and requested quite legitimately from his colleague that the situation be straightened out so that all these Canadians who pay taxes without being entitled to the corresponding benefit under this social program will be treated fairly.

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre Bussieres (Minister of National Revenue):
subtopic: REQUEST FOR EXPLANATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not see why the Hon. Member is asking me this question. The Minister of State for Finance, who represents the Minister of Finance, is in the House, as is the Minister of Manpower and Immigration, who is responsible for the administration of the Unemployment Insurance Act.
The Minister of Revenue has some responsibility in the administration of the Acts which, as the Hon. Member is well aware, deal with the Department of Finance and certain other departments. However, it is not up to the Minister of Revenue to propose changes to the legislation referred to by the Hon. Member.

NATIONAL REVENUE
subsubtopic: RESPONSIBILITY FOR ISSUING THIRD PARTY DEMANDS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of National Revenue. speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre Bussieres (Minister of National Revenue):
subtopic: NATIONAL REVENUE
subsubtopic: RESPONSIBILITY FOR ISSUING THIRD PARTY DEMANDS

subtopic: ENVIRONMENTAL AFFAIRS
ENVIRONMENTAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: AUTOMOBILE EMISSION HEARINGS-NON-APPEARANCE OF DEPARTMENTAL OFFICIALS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Transport. Last week the acid rain subcommittee of this House met in Toronto to hear briefs concerning automobile emissions. Representatives of the Minister's Department were asked to appear and give their position with respect to present standards and possible changes. Nobody from the Department turned up. Nobody offered any apologies. The Committee of Members of the House of Com-

March 13, 1984
Oral Questions
mons was treated with absolute contempt by the Minister's Department. Would the Minister like to explain why?

subtopic: ENVIRONMENTAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: AUTOMOBILE EMISSION HEARINGS-NON-APPEARANCE OF DEPARTMENTAL OFFICIALS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would first like to clarify the remarks made by the Hon. Member. In fact there was a member of the Department of Transport at the hearings, as an observer. Second, I had communicated with the Chairman of the Committee at an earlier date indicating that we would not be in a position to appear before the committee until such time as we had an opportunity to examine the studies that were under preparation. These studies were tabled just last week. We will now undertake careful consideration of them and consult with the appropriate bodies, as both my colleague, the Minister of the Environment, and I indicated publicly. Certainly there was no intention to have any disrespect for the committee. I will be very happy to appear before the committee. We will when we have something to say and a position to put forward.

subtopic: MINISTER'S ROLE
MINISTER'S ROLE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister's servant who appeared was far too frightened to say a word.
Was it the Minister's direct instructions that kept anybody from his Department from coming before a parliamentary sub-committee of Members of the House of Commons? Most certainly we did not have any information that the Minister had declined to come or declined to have any of his people there, nor was any reason given. Why did the Minister allow a situation to exist where a House of Commons committee of Members of Parliament that asked for representatives of the Department to come before it was absolutely refused? subtopic: MINISTER'S ROLE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I want to say to the Hon. Member for Vancouver South that I think he is jumping to conclusions. It may be the practice in his Party to let prejudice interfere with the facts. I prefer to make decisions based upon a proper examination of the studies that are available.

subtopic: MINISTER'S ROLE
speechtext: It means you are running for the leadership.

subtopic: MINISTER'S ROLE
speechtext: It was certainly our intention, and it would be my intention very happily so, to appear before the Committee when we are in a position to do so. That means having the opportunity to see what the studies say and determine what kind of standards would be appropriate to alleviate the situation. That kind of message was communicated to the Chairman of the Committee.

NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of National Defence. When the Minister served in his former position with respect to the Canadian frigate program, he made a statement. Now as the Minister for National Defence can he assure this House that of those contracts that have been let for the patrol frigate program fully two-thirds have been awarded to Canadian firms?

subtopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I can advise the hon. gentleman that, yes, we are meeting the target that had been set at the time the contract was signed. speakername: Hon.   J.-J. Blais@Minister of National Defence

subtopic: REQUEST THAT MINISTER TABLE LIST OF CONTRACTS
speechtext:

I will be pleased to provide the Hon. Member with as much information as can be made available, taking into account some commercial confidentialities that have to be maintained.
March 13, 1984
speakername: Hon.   J.-J. Blais@Minister of National Defence

Mr. Speaker, it is with immense pleasure that I rise to second the motion moved by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) just a moment ago. The House is in the process of uniquely honouring a unique Canadian. Throughout his 38 years the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) has graced the political process in our country, I think for two reasons. One is that he has been a man passionately committed in his political life, not simply to the abstract principles of social democracy, but to the details of reform for pensioners, to the details of reform for the poor, to the details of achieving equality for women. He has been a man who has seen that the parliamentary process is used, and passionately used, to bring about concrete change and improvement in the living conditions of ordinary people.
Second, and perhaps of greater importance in terms of the reason all Parties in the House are honouring him today, Stanley Knowles has seen the importance of the civilizing process of Parliament itself and has accepted this, I think more deeply than any other Member of Parliament during his time. He has well understood the unwritten rule of parliamentary democracy, which is that the deeply felt divisions that exist in society would be expressed violently ultimately if it were not for the civilizing process of parliamentary, democratic change. Throughout his life, Stanley Knowles has well understood that and has had that important lesson to teach the rest of us. His passionate commitment to the rules of this House has not been a fetish concern with irrelevant tradition. It has been a concern with the fundamentals of democratic change. That is what Stanley Knowles is all about.
On behalf of my colleagues, I thank the Prime Minister most directly for this initiative on his part. I was not able to be here about a week ago when other things were said about the Prime Minister's retirement. If I had been here, I would have made some deeply-felt, positive remarks about the Prime Minister. I would have been more sparing on those matters on which I disagree. I want to stress that this is an act of unqualified generosity on the part of the Prime Minister which has received the support which it ought to have from all Members of the House. For that I thank him on behalf of my colleagues.
I also want to refer to his observation that the man we are honouring today is wearing a rose. The Prime Minister suggested that, just as Stanley Knowles referred to the early days when the Prime Minister truly was a wise person, perhaps in his latter years Mr. Knowles had changed his political views. I simply want to say to the Prime Minister that Stanley is elderly, but he is not senile!
I conclude more graciously by once again saying thank you to Members of all other Parties in this House who have joined with us in honouring this truly distinguished Canadian.

Mr. Speaker, I was very interested in a number of points which the Hon. Member for Kootenay East-Revelstoke (Mr. Parker) made, but I am particularly interested in what he has said on other occasions as well dealing with moving coal that has very low sulphur content from the Kootenays, British Columbia and presumably Alberta to markets in eastern Canada for hydro purposes and the like. I am interested in those remarks for three reasons. The first reason I am interested in is that if we are to do something serious about acid rain, we will have to use the kind of coal to which the Hon. Member refers rather than the coal with high sulphur content which we are buying from the United States.
Second, I agree with the Hon. Member that the coal to which he refers is a Canadian product. If there is no great difference in cost, particularly when adding in the cost of reducing the sulphur content of the American coal to prevent acid rain, I would be very interested in seeing his coal brought to market in the east.
The third reason I am interested, and I must say this very strongly, is that we in Thunder Bay have developed a major coal terminal. If we were to move coal through that terminal the way I think we would, that coal terminal would become almost as large as the one in Vancouver. Certainly jobs on the railways in Atikokan, Thunder Bay and throughout the country would be created if this happened.
I think we on this side of the House are very interested in the kind of proposition made by the Hon. Member. I would ask him if he can give us a little more detail than he has furnished up to now regarding the expected costs of this operation, bearing in mind that some very large savings can be made, particularly in terms of environmental savings and savings through the creation of jobs. If those jobs are not created, we will have to use the UIC and other forms of federal assistance to support the people who will not have those jobs. If we can create more jobs, it will be a great advantage. I would ask the Hon. Member to give us a little more detail on this subject.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1984-85 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to answer the question put to me by the Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Atikokan (Mr. McRae). There has been an extensive study done on this matter by the United Mine
Workers of America, District No. 18, being the Submission on Canadian Use of Western Canada Coal of June 15, 1983. That study was presented to the Ministry of Transport which has been looking at it. From the information which was supplied to us through a conference of coal producers and others, that Department is looking at the possibility of a requirement for a subsidy in the neighbourhood of about $23 a tonne.
At the present time about three million or four million tonnes of western Canada coal is coming from Byron Creek and Alberta and going to Ontario. That coal is mainly being shipped to eastern Canada for blending in order to stop the kinds of things we are talking about with regard to acid rain. As the Hon. Member knows, we are shipping some coal from the west at the present time but another 16 million tonnes of coal with tremendously high sulphur content is coming in from the United States.
As the Hon. Member has stated, this scheme would do away with a large amount of unemployment. We would also have the opportunity of blending coal to meet the needs of Ontario Hydro and steel mills in Ontario. As well, we know at this time that some contracts contain minimum and maximum clauses, and even if we were dealing with the minimum clauses in those contracts, we could immediately begin, to ship in the neighbourhood of another five million tonnes of coal from western Canada, whether it be from British Columbia, Alberta or Saskatchewan.

As I suggested, the coal we are using produces sulphur emissions of 800 per cent whereas the coal in western Canada has a sulphur content of .05 per cent. The coal that is coming in from the Appalachians has a sulphur content of anywhere between 4 per cent and 5 per cent. The ramifications and opportunities are tremendous.
In the communities of the Kootenays and in Alberta resolutions were put before the committees requesting that a study be done on the cost of transporting this coal, and that the study look at the possibility of the cost being shared equally. speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. The job of French translation and interpretation will be made much easier now if I can say something.
I would like to address the question of the borrowing in which our country has become involved by starting out with the perspective that this country is unique in the world. It ought not to have the economic problems it does. This is a resource-rich nation, one which has been blessed with virtually every resource one could possibly imagine. We are wanting in almost nothing. We have an educated population, we have standards of health, transportation and communication which should advance this nation very much into the forefront of the industrialized nations of the world. Yet, Sir, it is against this background that we recognize that Canada, with all of this enormous natural wealth, is borrowing at a rate parallel to that of Brazil, Mexico and other Latin American countries. Our debt, Sir, is one of the highest of the industrialized nations. We are a country which borrows, borrows and borrows.
In this particular Parliament, we have had presented to us Bill C-30 for $12 billion; Bill C-59 for $14 billion; Bill C-lll for $6.6 billion; Bill C-125 for $7 billion; Bill C-128 for $4 billion; Bill C-143 for $19 billion; Bill C-151 for $10.71 billion, and now we are debating Bill C-21 for the highest amount, that is, $29.55 billion. That is a total of $102 billion of borrowing in one Parliament. While I recognize that that amount is to be spread over a four-year period, the truth of the matter is that we are borrowing more in this particular Bill than the sum that made up the total budget of the Government when the present Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) came to power. We are borrowing more than double that amount.
Most people in the private sector of Canada are intuitively aware that borrowing is not automatically wrong. However, when we borrow for the purposes of making money it has much more credence than borrowing just for our common pleasure. It makes sense for a farmer to borrow to expand his land base or to buy machinery and for a store owner to borrow to expand his operation because they are borrowing on an economic principle, which is to make their equity grow.
This Government is now, Sir, borrowing to pay for the debt of its past borrowings. One-third of the tax dollars collected are used to pay the service of our national debt. Every time a taxpayer anywhere in Canada pays $3 to the Government of Canada, one of those dollars is used to pay interest on that
Borrowing Authority Act
accumulated borrowing. We have become a part of a treadmill of debt from which this Government has found no way to remove itself.
We are now some $180 billion in total debt as a nation. One of the difficulties, which I find, Sir, is that while the notion of democracy is something which is near and dear to the hearts of most Canadians, and while the concept of democracy implies that the people govern themselves, we are now dealing with numbers so large that on these issues the people, in essence, simply give up. They do not know what a billion dollars is and they do not know the implication of the increase from $15 billion of borrowing to $29.2 billion of borrowing. Therefore, in some attempt to simplify it, or at least to make it understandable, let me underline just how much a billion dollars is. A billion dollars means that if you spent $100 a minute for every minute of every hour for 24 hours a day for seven days a week, it would take you 19 years to spend a billion dollars. That, Sir, is the magnitude of that number.
Yet, Sir, Canada is locked in in an undisciplined way to the American economy following the difficulties here, which are also present in that nation. That nation has a debt which will approach $1.8 trillion by March of 1985. The amount is so staggering that people cannot use the latex of their minds to stretch around its circumference. But that debt, Sir, means that if $1,000 bills were stacked one on top of the other, it would make a column going up into the sky that is 120 miles high. As a Member of Parliament from Alberta, every time I fly between my constituency and Ottawa, I am flying at a height of approximately 40,000 feet. That seems to me like a long way up. Yet, that distance is just a little more than seven miles. If we ran into that column of the debt of the United States there would be still 117 miles of debt above us. All I can say is that we are dealing with numbers that are enormous in scope.
North America must get off the treadmill of borrowing, at least borrowing to the extent we are now. Generally speaking, we have taken the perspective that we can borrow in a healthy economy up to about 2 per cent of our Gross National Product. Canada today is borrowing between 5 per cent and 8 per cent of our Gross National Product. The ratio of debt to the strength of our economy is such that we are certainly extending ourselves beyond the capacity of our GNP to grow. That is the important fact to bear in mind, because when we borrow to improve our standard of living today, we are mortgaging the future of tomorrow's generation. If we borrow beyond the capacity of the Gross National Product to grow, future generations will be born with a debt. A new citizen born today inherits a debt of about $1,700 at the moment of birth. This treadmill must be broken, because this borrowing of $29 billion is such that it creates a real hardship for our citizens today and for those to come tomorrow.
A speaker from the Government side projected earlier today the view that the purpose of the borrowing was, to a large extent, to provide make-work projects through Canada Works,

March 13, 1984
Borrowing Authority Act
New Elorizons projects and community development programs, and is therefore justified. I suggest to him-I believe it was the Eton. Member for Lachine (Mr. Blaker)-that he read the latest issue of Time Magazine, that of March 5, 1984, which talks about the deficit and borrowing in the U.S. The simple conclusion one can draw from that article is that there are three specific areas in which borrowing does significant damage to a free enterprise economy: the effect on interest rates, employment and inflation.
We have to recognize that it is not only governments that borrow money. The private sector, farmers, fishermen, businessmen and manufacturers, all seek ways to increase their capital. However, when the Government goes to the market and asks for $29.2 billion, it has the effect of driving up interest rates for everyone else. That is precisely the situation we are in today. Interest rates, while lower than a year ago, are still artificially high, certainly when compared to the average over the past decade. The real creators of wealth, the private sector, are attempting to build their businesses and create jobs, but they cannot do that efficiently because the Government has taken all the cheap money for Government services, which is the least efficient use of capital. Because interest rates are up there has been a decrease, as the statistics show, in the establishment of new businesses, with a resulting negative impact on employment in Canada.
As I said earlier, Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member across the way took the position that when the Government borrows money, we are able to supply make-work projects. I, like other Members, will apply for the money for make-work projects in my constituency when it is there, but I hope the day will soon arrive when we no longer have make-work projects, because it does not do us any good to pay a student to paint a hall somewhere after which he is out of work again. What we need to do is to build permanent factories, create permanent jobs, which in turn creates the wealth from which the Government collects tax dollars. That is the way you pay for the social needs of this country. We have to build a bigger pie.
I do not understand for a single moment how the little island of Japan, with a few resources such as fish, tin and nothing else except an educated people, has the second largest economy in the world. Sir, I started that sentence wrong. I said I do not know how. Well, I do know how. They do it through productivity; their people work. But what do we do here? We create every stumbling block you can imagine to discourage people from working. We put interest rates up so high that no one is going to borrow money to develop his business. We have Revenue Canada which acts as though it were the Gestapo, chasing people to try to gather the money for the Government of Canada to spend. When you see the frustration of constituents in trying to deal with the Government, trying to get through the red tape and inefficiencies, knowing that when they pay their taxes $1 in every $3 goes to pay for past borrowings, it is no wonder the economy is grinding down.
It makes you wonder what the Japanese would do if they ever got hold of this country. Here we are, Sir, blessed with an educated people, one third of the world's fresh water, tremendous natural resources, and we cannot put our act together. It seems to me the message is clear: there is something wrong with the Government because the management of this country is obviously faltering.
It would be interesting, Mr. Speaker, if we could get more Liberals to speak on this issue. We have $29 billion in borrowing authority being sought, and hardly any of them stand up to comment. To repeat, economists generally agree that we can safely borrow up to about 2 per cent of our Gross National Product. We can borrow more when we have an expanding GNP. But here we are hovering around 5 per cent to 8 per cent of the GNP and the money is not being used for productive purposes.
It behooves me to say we are on the Turner turnpike. It was the former Minister of Finance, John Turner, who started us on this road. He introduced the greatest spending of any Minister of Finance to that date in history. It was John Turner who gave us the largest debt we had until that time. It was his Budget which compelled succeeding Ministers of Finance to take the same road. Therefore, while there are those who would appreciate not having a Liberal leadership convention, who believe that John Turner should simply be anointed leader, the truth is that this country is in this desperate economic position because of John Turner. He started us down that road, and the Government has been going in that direction ever since. We have failed to pay our debts. As a nation, we believe falsely that the next generation could pick up this debt. Some day the pillars will crumble, the economy will collapse, and the future generation will have to pay the debt. People in private life recognize that.
Governments have two hopes. The first hope they have is that there will be a period of extended inflation. That is one way to cure a debt. Certainly it is an unsatisfactory hope to have. The other hope is that there will be a total collapse of the economy. I should add that there is a third hope, which is that the bills will be paid. In 16 years there has been no effort made by the Government to take the position of paying its bills. The debts continue to grow, and today we are just short of $200 billion in total accumulated debt.
I see you are giving me a high sign, Mr. Speaker. It would be most unfortunate if 1 were cut off now as I am not yet through the first two pages of my comments. I am just warming up to what the Government is doing to us. We must bear in mind that Canada is now one of the world's most indebted nations. We rank with Brazil and Mexico. We are indebted on a larger percentage of our total wealth than are most other nations in the world.
Earlier in my speech I said that by March of 1985 it is projected that the United States will have a debt of $1.8 trillion. That is a column of $1,000 bills 120 miles high. Members on the Government side may shrug and suggest that that is not the debt in Canada. There are well over 200 million people in the United States and only about 24 million in Canada. Canada's per capita debt is 50 per cent higher than
March 13, 1984

that in the United States. Based on a per citizen average, our debt is much higher than theirs.
I have caught sight of your signal, Mr. Speaker, and I will sit down soon. It is interesting that for four years the United States has made every effort possible to turn around its debt situation. That is largely a measure of the campaign which is going on now. My final comment is that Canada must get control of its debt. It must decrease the amount that it is borrowing, or an unnecessary peril will befall all of tomorrow's children of this great and blessed land. They should not have to bear that burden.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to make one point with respect to Bill C-21, which deals with the borrowing authority of the Government. This entire debate relating to our borrowing authority boils down to one question: is the Government's approach to encouraging economic recovery the proper approach? In other words, from a global point of view, will the expenditures of the Government as provided for in the current Budget encourage the recovery of our economy? I believe that our Budget will lead to economic recovery.
There are various ways in which we can look at this problem. I find it far too easy to single out certain items in the Budget and indicate that they are not sufficient or wrong. It is far too easy for us to ignore the medium or long-term effects of the benefits of a Budget, particularly the one we are studying today.
Naturally, we are looking toward a reduction in our deficit, as is any Member of the Opposition. We would like to see the deficit eradicated as soon as possible. There is more than one way to approach this problem. One approach is to slash expenditures and cut various programs, with the eventual hope of arriving at a balanced set of books. We do not believe in that approach. We believe that the only way to balance our Budget is by improving the productivity of the country to the point where revenues will increase in an amount sufficient to meet our expenditures. Increased productivity is also necessary in order to improve our competitive position in the world. We face problems if we cannot sell our products around the world.
The main purpose of our Budget is to increase productivity. We intend to do this by proposing several measures. First, we will attempt to simplify the tax system. As Hon. members are aware, that system has become so complicated that even our expert tax lawyers will no longer give an opinion on it. Second, we will attempt to initiate steps that will increase confidence in the country, including that of the private sector and of investors whom we will try to entice to Canada. At the same time we want to establish some confidence in the workers of the country. In that respect we will improve our pension system.
One of my objectives when I came here five years ago was to examine the possibility of improving the lot of Canadians over the long term. I recognized full well that we had become far too dependent on the state and that this could not continue over the long term.
I am very proud to have served as vice-chairman on the task force on pension reform, and am deeply grateful to the Government for accepting our recommendations, which will help Canadians to help themselves. They provide the means and the mechanism by which Canadians can look after their own problems in old age. In the next ten or twenty years I think the items contained in the Budget with respect to pension reform will be of great, great benefit to this country.
By encouraging our youth, which we are doing through measures in the Budget, I think we are at the same time improving productivity. By increasing the security we are offering to home owners through an insurance scheme which will guarantee interest rates that home owners will be paying we are increasing confidence and productivity.
Some of our sales tax changes will improve the climate for business. We are proposing some tax assistance for employee profit participation plans, which is another way of improving productivity. We are proposing tax assistance for employee stock option plans, which is yet another improvement to productivity.
In short, the fact that the debate has come this far is testimony that Members opposite, to my mind, have either not read the Budget or, if they have, have not understood it. I think that because we are asking for borrowing authority based on a Budget which is reasonable and predicated on arriving at the same end as that proposed by Members opposite, it is a waste of time to discuss the amounts involved in it, because these have nothing to do with what will be spent. That will come through in the Estimates. I rest my case, Mr. Speaker.

This time the borrowing Bill is the largest in Canadian history. Just a moment ago the Hon. Member opposite asked if they were not doing something right. They are doing everything wrong.
In the first session of this Parliament the Government came to us seven times for additional borrowing authority. That is truly a remarkable record of fiscal management, accountability and responsibility.
On May 10, 1983, during debate on the last borrowing Bill I noted that the Government had approached the House only three weeks after bringing in a Budget which added $31 billion to our existing gross national debt of a staggering, and I say staggering, $134 billion. With this Bill it wants to increase that burden by an additional $14.7 billion. As I said, here we go again! Three weeks after the Budget, the Government is seeking to borrow an amount which is almost equal to the entire gross debt of $31 billion when the present Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) took office. Now the Government wants $29.55 billion.
This borrowing should be exactly halved to make any sense whatsoever. It should be no more than $15 billion. Right now there is $5 billion in their till. It is more than enough to take these wastrels to November 1 at least. What an accomplishment this Government has! What a legacy the Prime Minister leaves to his successor, to all Canadians and to our future generations! Our children are buried in debt, inundated. That is what it is all about.
As I said, the Government does not really need the money because a new Government Leader, unfortunately a Liberal, will take office shortly after June 17, and this Government's Budget will no longer be the Budget of the Government. Leadership candidates in Liberal ranks are already making statements about government waste and profligacy. The two of them walked right into that trap the other morning. We heard the Hon. Member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) take them apart inch by inch and piece by piece. The Minister of Justice (Mr. MacGuigan), of all people, said that the Government's response to problems was to throw money at them. The Minister of State for Economic and Regional Development (Mr. Johnston) questioned universal programs. It was not us, it was the Government. We are the Party of free enterprise with a social conscience.
What could happen to the country? The new leader could go to the people in August, which of course would mean the election of a new Progressive Conservative Government. Or he could wait, prevaricate and finally go in 1985, and obviously the new Leader would not need money then because he would have to bring in a new budget anyway. The most we on this side of the House could countenance is $15 billion.
Bill C-21 provides the authority to borrow up to an additional $29.55 billion. Of the $29.6 billion projected deficit, only $25.55 billion must be borrowed, after taking into account non-budgetary sources of $4.05 billion. It was not long ago that C. D. Howe said, "What is a million?" The new C. D. Howe of this era is P. E. "What's a Billion" Prime Minister. What is a billion? the Hon. Member for Crowfoot (Mr. Malone) gave his definition of it. I should like to give a few examples to Canadians as well in terms that even a Prime Minister with no interest in economics whatsoever could understand.
A billion minutes ago Christ was walking on earth. A billion hours ago our ancestors lived in caves. A billion dollars ago was last week in terms of the way the Government sees things. What about $31.5 billion? Laid end to end in a line, that many dollar bills would stretch for three billion miles, or the equivalent of 304 round trips on the Trans-Canada Highway, or six round trips to the moon. On the other hand, 31.5 billion one dollar bills, stacked one on top of the other, would reach a height of 108 miles. Stacked separately, the Government could put 317 piles of dollar bills as high as the CN Tower in various cities and towns across Canada. Simcoe South could use one of those piles because it did not receive a cent from the Special Employment Initiatives Program, the slush fund of the Liberal Party. This is probably why the Government wants those extra $15 billion to $19 billion. All these towers could stand as monuments to Liberal fiscal irresponsibility. The House does not have to take my word for it. Hon. Members just have to read the reports of the Auditor General over the years of uncontrolled, runaway, profligate spending by the people across the aisle.
Bill C-21 is just another indication that the Government has given up on the concept of accountability. It needs no more than $15 billion, and it throws a red herring at us of $29.55 billion, part of a so-called $4 billion contingency fund. We are not told how this money will be spent. Will it be for one of those job-creation programs, which in reality is a job-replacement program? Will it be for another local initiatives program where every Liberal riding gets another poke at $500,000? The cracks are widening across the way. The Government would like to show us as being opposed to social programs when in reality we are the champions of them.
We are considering the largest borrowing Bill in the history of the country. The requirements in the Bill are equal to 91 per cent of forecast personal savings this year. The cupboards will be bare when the private sector comes looking for funds to expand, invest and create new jobs. We will be so poor if we let them go at it one more time that we will not be able to raise
March 13, 1984

umbrellas. One more go with this outfit, and I just do not know what will happen to our wonderful country of Canada.
Even this is not the total picture. The phalanx of Crown corporations do not require special authority from Parliament to raise funds in financial markets, nor must they tell Parliament what their financial requirements will be. Deficit financing is the legacy of the present Prime Minister's Government.
The Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Evans) stated the Liberal position quite clearly on February 22, 1983, long before we were thinking about this debate, when he told the House that "a deficit is no more and no less than an increase in future tax liabilities". He went on to say:
The present economic situation being as it is, I believe that the best way to stimulate the economy and maintain the income support programs that are necessary in our economy is to use the deficit.
That is the philosophy of the Government. The Liberals have certainly used the deficit; however, the only thing that has been stimulated has been the deficit itself. By their policies our dollar is softer than pita bread dough.
As Hon. Members are aware, interest rates are now rising rapidly. Last week one-year Treasury bills moved from 10.44 per cent to 10.95 per cent, an increase of over 50 bases points or about one-half of one per cent. The present net federal debt matures within about 2.5 years and its essential following interest rate debt. The effect of last week's increase alone increased the cost of carrying the $150 billion net debt by $750 million. This "little" increase totally shattered the Budget of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde), in my opinion.
On a national accounts basis, spending has climbed from $12.6 billion in 1968, a year that I would like to forget, to an estimated $107.5 billion this year. That is an increase of 773 per cent. Most of that increase has occurred since the Liberals were re-elected in February 1980, believe it or not. Relative to fiscal 1979-80, spending has risen by 97 per cent on a national accounts basis. There has been 97 per cent increase in spending since that day in 1980 when the Prime Minister stated, "We will not allow the deficit to rise any higher from any new program we announce". Let us keep that high-sounding promise in mind as we review the situation today.
By the end of this fiscal year the gross debt will be $190 billion. It was $31 billion when the present Prime Minister took office. The net debt this year will be $150.7 billion compared with $17.7 billion in 1968. The Budget of three weeks ago will add $110.8 billion to the net debt over the next four years. Remember, we have an increase in excise tax coming in October. The net national debt will have quadrupled to $261.5 billion in only eight years. Is it any wonder they have no qualms about walking in here and asking for an extra measly $29.5 billion? Government spending is now 26 per cent of GNP. How silly can we get? The cost of servicing this shameful debt in fiscal 1983-84 is $18.1 billion, rising to $24.7 billion by 1988, an increase of 17 times the cost at the time when the Prime Minister took office.
Borrowing Authority Act
In 1984-85, service costs will reach $20.4 billion, or $800 per capita, or $1,900 per taxpayer. As has been pointed out, this is double that in the United States. Is it any wonder that Revenue Canada must stoop to such depths to wring every dollar from Canadians and then some? The cases on my desk alone are horrifying.
The only difference between this Government and Jesse James is that the latter used a gun. People knew exactly what he wanted and how he planned to get it. With this Government, most Canadians do not have a clue where we are going or how we are going to pay the cost of getting there. As I said, this Bill does not tell us one thing about how the money will be spent.
The enormous cost of servicing the debt interferes with private sector borrowing. In the 1983 calendar year, federal Government borrowing accounted for 58 per cent of the net new security issues placed in Canada. This forces interest rates up for the private sector borrowers who must compete for what little is left after the Government gets its share. As long as this continues, there is no way that the private sector can bring about an enduring economic recovery. It is obvious that the Government cannot do it. The result is the economic quagmire in which we find ourselves.
In its submission to the Macdonald Commission on the economy, the Bank of Montreal points out the danger to private sector-lead growth stemming from the Government's deficit financing policy. It says that the most likely way to achieve higher rates of business investment over the medium term is to foster a decline in real rates of interest, a task that will be difficult to realize without a reduction in the federal Government's ever increasing claim on a limited pool of savings. It says also that without a reduction of the structural deficit, the resultant higher real rates could negate many of the tax incentives aimed at promoting business investment. John Bulloch of the CFIB pointed out another aspect of the problem in a speech last year when he said:
We still have to face the fundamental fact that we are looking at core deficits in our society that cannot be financed unless we curb its costs. To try to tax people for that amount would blow us out of the water as an economic power in terms of competing with the United States.
Note the references to core and structural deficits. The huge debt has become a fact of economic life in Canada. It seems that these ever-increasing borrowing Bills are here to stay, at least until the next election. That is what 16 years of this Prime Minister's style of socialism has done for us, started by the man who has the desire to replace him. It is too late for a new Liberal leader to make any difference. What is needed is a new Progressive Conservative Government committed to reducing the deficit, getting spending under control and restoring confidence-a word that Members opposite do not know the meaning of-among the business community. In its 1983 year-end economic assessment, the Canadian Chamber of Commerce noted:
In order to undertake long-term investment, business must be convinced that inflation and interest rates will not surge again. A clearly defined Government commitment to spending restraint and deficit reduction would go a long way

March 13, 1984
